Hung be the heavens with black, yield day to night! / Comets, importing change of times and states, / Brandish your crystal tresses in the sky, / And with them scourge the bad revolting stars / That have consented unto Henry's death! / King Henry the Fifth, too famous to live long! / England ne'er lost a king of so much worth.

Let the skies be hung with black and day give way to night! Comets, which foretell changes in times and states, wave your bright tails across the sky and whip the wicked, rebellious stars that agreed to Henry's death! King Henry the Fifth, too famous to live long! England never lost a king so worthy.

England ne'er had a king until his time. / Virtue he had, deserving to command: / His brandish'd sword did blind men with his beams: / His arms spread wider than a dragon's wings; / His sparkling eyes, replete with wrathful fire, / More dazzled and drove back his enemies / Than mid-day sun fierce bent against their faces. / What should I say? his deeds exceed all speech: / He ne'er lift up his hand but conquered.

England never had a true king until him. He had virtue fit to command; his flashing sword blinded men with its light; his arms spread wider than a dragon's wings; his sparkling eyes, full of angry fire, dazzled and drove back his enemies more than the midday sun blazing in their faces. What can I say? His deeds are beyond words. He never raised his hand without conquering.

We mourn in black: why mourn we not in blood? / Henry is dead and never shall revive: / Upon a wooden coffin we attend, / And death's dishonourable victory / We with our stately presence glorify, / Like captives bound to a triumphant car. / What! shall we curse the planets of mishap / That plotted thus our glory's overthrow? / Or shall we think the subtle-witted French / Conjurers and sorcerers, that afraid of him / By magic verses have contriv'd his end?

We mourn in black; why don't we mourn in blood? Henry is dead and will never come back to life. We walk beside a wooden coffin and, with our grand presence, glorify death's shameful victory, like prisoners tied to a conqueror's chariot. What! Shall we curse the unlucky planets that plotted the end of our glory? Or shall we think the cunning French are conjurers and sorcerers who, afraid of him, killed him with magic spells?

He was a king bless'd of the King of kings; / Unto the French the dreadful judgment-day / So dreadful will not be as was his sight. / The battles of the Lord of hosts he fought: / The Church's prayers made him so prosperous.

He was a king blessed by the King of kings. To the French, Judgement Day itself will not be as terrifying as the sight of him was. He fought the battles of the Lord of hosts; the Church's prayers made him so successful.
The church! where is it? Had not churchmen pray'd, / His thread of life had not so soon decay'd: / None do you like but an effeminate prince, / Whom, like a school-boy, you may over-awe.
The Church! Where is it? If churchmen hadn't prayed, his life would not have ended so soon. You like nothing but a weak, soft prince whom you can bully like a schoolboy.
Gloucester, whate'er we like, thou art Protector, / And lookest to command the Prince and realm. / Thy wife is proud; she holdeth thee in awe, / More than God or religious churchmen may.
Gloucester, whatever we like, you are Protector, and you aim to rule the Prince and the kingdom. Your wife is proud; she has more control over you than God or the clergy do.
Name not religion, for thou lov'st the flesh, / And ne'er throughout the year to church thou go'st, / Except it be to pray against thy foes.
Don't talk about religion, for you love the pleasures of the flesh, and you never go to church all year except to pray against your enemies.

Cease, cease these jars and rest your minds in peace: / Let's to the altar: heralds, wait on us: / Instead of gold, we'll offer up our arms; / Since arms avail not, now that Henry's dead. / Posterity, await for wretched years, / When at their mothers' moist eyes babes shall suck, / Our isle be made a marish of salt tears, / And none but women left to wail the dead. / Henry the Fifth, thy ghost I invocate: / Prosper this realm, keep it from civil broils, / Combat with adverse planets in the heavens! / A far more glorious star thy soul will make / Than Julius Caesar or bright—

Stop, stop these quarrels and calm yourselves. Let's go to the altar. Heralds, attend us. Instead of gold, we'll offer up our weapons, since weapons are no use now Henry is dead. Future ages, expect miserable years, when babies will suck at their mothers' tear-wet eyes, our island will become a marsh of salt tears, and only women will be left to mourn the dead. Henry the Fifth, I call on your spirit: make this kingdom prosper, keep it from civil wars, fight the hostile planets in the heavens! Your soul will make a far more glorious star than Julius Caesar or bright—

My honourable lords, health to you all! / Sad tidings bring I to you out of France, / Of loss, of slaughter, and discomfiture: / Guienne, Champagne, Rheims, Orleans, / Paris, Guysors, Poictiers, are all quite lost.
My honourable lords, health to you all! I bring sad news from France of loss, slaughter and defeat. Guienne, Champagne, Rheims, Orleans, Paris, Gisors and Poitiers are all lost.
What say'st thou, man, before dead Henry's corse? / Speak softly; or the loss of those great towns / Will make him burst his lead and rise from death.
What are you saying, man, in front of dead Henry's body? Speak quietly, or the loss of those great towns will make him burst his lead coffin and rise from the dead.
Is Paris lost? Is Rouen yielded up / If Henry were recall'd to life again, / These news would cause him once more yield the ghost.
Is Paris lost? Has Rouen surrendered? If Henry were brought back to life, this news would make him die again.
How were they lost? What treachery was us'd?
How were they lost? What treachery was used?

No treachery; but want of men and money. / Amongst the soldiers this is muttered, / That here you maintain several factions, / And whilst a field should be dispatch'd and fought, / You are disputing of your generals: / One would have lingering wars with little cost; / Another would fly swift, but wanteth wings; / A third thinks, without expense at all, / By guileful fair words peace may be obtain'd. / Awake, awake, English nobility! / Let not sloth dim your honours new-begot: / Cropp'd are the flower-de-luces in your arms; / Of England's coat one half is cut away.

No treachery, but a shortage of men and money. The soldiers are muttering that here at home you keep up rival factions, and while a battle should be fought and won, you are arguing about your generals. One wants a long war that costs little; another wants to move fast but has no means to; a third thinks peace can be won by clever, smooth words, without any spending at all. Wake up, wake up, English nobles! Don't let idleness tarnish your newly won honours. The French lilies have been cut from your coat of arms; half of England's shield has been hacked away.
Were our tears wanting to this funeral, / These tidings would call forth their flowing tides.
If our tears were lacking at this funeral, this news would call them out in floods.

Me they concern; Regent I am of France. / Give me my steeled coat. I'll fight for France. / Away with these disgraceful wailing robes! / Wounds will I lend the French instead of eyes, / To weep their intermissive miseries.

This news concerns me: I am Regent of France. Give me my steel armour. I'll fight for France. Away with these shameful mourning clothes! I'll give the French wounds to weep with instead of eyes, to cry over their own endless sufferings.

Lords, view these letters full of bad mischance. / France is revolted from the English quite, / Except some petty towns of no import: / The Dauphin Charles is crowned king in Rheims; / The Bastard of Orleans with him is join'd; / Reignier, Duke of Anjou, doth take his part; / The Duke of Alencon flieth to his side.

Lords, read these letters full of bad news. France has rebelled completely against the English, except for a few unimportant towns. The Dauphin Charles has been crowned king in Rheims; the Bastard of Orleans has joined him; Reignier, Duke of Anjou, supports him; the Duke of Alencon is hurrying to his side.
The Dauphin crowned king! all fly to him! / O, whither shall we fly from this reproach?
The Dauphin crowned king! Everyone running to him! Oh, where can we run to escape this shame?
We will not fly, but to our enemies' throats. / Bedford, if thou be slack, I'll fight it out.
We won't run anywhere but at our enemies' throats. Bedford, if you are slow, I'll fight it out myself.
Gloucester, why doubt'st thou of my forwardness? / An army have I muster'd in my thoughts, / Wherewith already France is overrun.
Gloucester, why do you doubt my eagerness? I have already raised an army in my mind and with it overrun France.
My gracious lords, to add to your laments, / Wherewith you now bedew King Henry's hearse, / I must inform you of a dismal fight / Betwixt the stout Lord Talbot and the French.
My gracious lords, to add to the grief with which you now wet King Henry's coffin, I must tell you of a terrible battle between brave Lord Talbot and the French.
What! wherein Talbot overcame? is't so?
What! Talbot won? Is that it?

O, no; wherein Lord Talbot was o'erthrown: / The circumstance I'll tell you more at large. / The tenth of August last this dreadful lord, / Retiring from the siege of Orleans, / Having full scarce six thousand in his troop, / By three and twenty thousand of the French / Was round encompassed and set upon. / No leisure had he to enrank his men; / He wanted pikes to set before his archers; / Instead whereof sharp stakes pluck'd out of hedges / They pitched in the ground confusedly, / To keep the horsemen off from breaking in. / More than three hours the fight continued; / Where valiant Talbot above human thought / Enacted wonders with his sword and lance: / Hundreds he sent to hell, and none durst stand him; / Here, there, and every where, enrag'd he slew: / The French exclaim'd, the devil was in arms; / All the whole army stood agaz'd on him. / His soldiers spying his undaunted spirit / A Talbot! a Talbot! cried out amain, / And rush'd into the bowels of the battle. / Here had the conquest fully been seal'd up, / If Sir John Fastolfe had not play'd the coward. / He, being in the vaward, plac'd behind / With purpose to relieve and follow them, / Cowardly fled, not having struck one stroke. / Hence grew the general wreck and massacre; / Enclosed were they with their enemies: / A base Walloon, to win the Dauphin's grace, / Thrust Talbot with a spear into the back; / Whom all France with their chief assembled strength / Durst not presume to look once in the face.

Oh no; Lord Talbot was defeated. I'll tell you the details. On the tenth of August last, as this fearsome lord was withdrawing from the siege of Orleans with barely six thousand men, he was surrounded and attacked by twenty-three thousand French. He had no time to draw up his men in ranks. He had no pikes to set in front of his archers, so instead they hammered sharp stakes pulled from hedges into the ground in a rough line to keep the cavalry from breaking in. The fight went on for more than three hours, and brave Talbot performed superhuman wonders with sword and lance. He sent hundreds to hell, and nobody dared stand against him. He killed in a rage here, there and everywhere. The French cried that the devil himself was fighting; the whole army stood staring at him. His soldiers, seeing his fearless spirit, shouted "A Talbot! A Talbot!" and charged into the heart of the battle. The victory would have been certain if Sir John Fastolfe had not acted the coward. He was in the vanguard, placed behind them to support and follow, but he ran away like a coward without striking a single blow. That caused the general disaster and slaughter: they were surrounded by enemies. A low-born Walloon, to win the Dauphin's favour, stabbed Talbot in the back with a spear, a man whom the whole of France with all its forces never dared look in the face.
Is Talbot slain? then I will slay myself, / For living idly here in pomp and ease, / Whilst such a worthy leader, wanting aid, / Unto his dastard foemen is betray'd.
Is Talbot dead? Then I'll kill myself for living here idle in luxury and comfort while such a worthy leader, without help, is handed over to his cowardly enemies.
O no, he lives; but is took prisoner, / And Lord Scales with him, and Lord Hungerford: / Most of the rest slaughter'd or took likewise.
Oh no, he's alive, but taken prisoner, and Lord Scales and Lord Hungerford with him. Most of the rest were killed or captured too.

His ransom there is none but I shall pay: / I'll hale the Dauphin headlong from his throne: / His crown shall be the ransom of my friend; / Four of their lords I'll change for one of ours. / Farewell, my masters; to my task will I; / Bonfires in France forthwith I am to make / To keep our great Saint George's feast withal: / Ten thousand soldiers with me I will take, / Whose bloody deeds shall make an Europe quake.

I alone will pay his ransom. I'll drag the Dauphin headfirst from his throne; his crown will be the ransom for my friend. I'll exchange four of their lords for one of ours. Goodbye, gentlemen; I'll get to my work. I must go to France at once to light bonfires for our great Saint George's feast. I'll take ten thousand soldiers whose bloody deeds will make all Europe tremble.

So you had need; for Orleans is besieg'd; / The English army is grown weak and faint: / The Earl of Salisbury craveth supply, / And hardly keeps his men from mutiny, / Since they, so few, watch such a multitude.

You'll need them, for Orleans is under siege. The English army has grown weak and tired. The Earl of Salisbury is begging for reinforcements and can barely keep his men from mutiny, since so few of them have to watch over so many.
Remember, lords, your oaths to Henry sworn, / Either to quell the Dauphin utterly, / Or bring him in obedience to your yoke.
Remember, lords, the oaths you swore to Henry: either to crush the Dauphin completely or bring him under your rule.
I do remember it, and here take my leave / To go about my preparation.
I do remember, and I'll say goodbye now to go and make my preparations.
I'll to the Tower with all the haste I can, / To view the artillery and munition; / And then I will proclaim young Henry king.
I'll go to the Tower as fast as I can to inspect the artillery and weapons, and then I'll proclaim young Henry king.
To Eltham will I, where the young King is, / Being ordain'd his special governor; / And for his safety there I'll best devise.
I'll go to Eltham, where the young King is, since I've been appointed his special guardian, and I'll arrange his safety there as best I can.

Each hath his place and function to attend: / I am left out; for me nothing remains. / But long I will not be Jack out of office: / The King from Eltham I intend to steal, / And sit at chiefest stern of public weal.
Everyone has his place and job to do; I am left out, nothing is left for me. But I won't be out of office for long. I intend to snatch the King away from Eltham and sit at the helm of the state.

Mars his true moving, even as in the heavens / So in the earth, to this day is not known: / Late did he shine upon the English side; / Now we are victors; upon us he smiles. / What towns of any moment but we have? / At pleasure here we lie near Orleans; / Otherwhiles the famish'd English, like pale ghosts, / Faintly besiege us one hour in a month.

Even now nobody knows the true movement of Mars, the god of war, on earth any more than in the heavens. Lately he shone on the English; now we are winning and he smiles on us. What important towns are there that we don't hold? We camp at our ease here near Orleans, while every so often the starving English, like pale ghosts, weakly besiege us for an hour a month.
They want their porridge and their fat bull beeves / Either they must be dieted like mules, / And have their provender tied to their mouths, / Or piteous they will look, like drowned mice.
They miss their porridge and their fat beef. Either they'll have to be fed like mules, with nosebags tied to their mouths, or they'll look pitiful, like drowned mice.

Let's raise the siege: why live we idly here? / Talbot is taken, whom we wont to fear: / Remaineth none but mad-brain'd Salisbury; / And he may well in fretting spend his gall, / Nor men nor money hath he to make war.

Let's break the siege. Why are we sitting here idle? Talbot, whom we used to fear, is captured. Only mad Salisbury is left, and he can fret away his anger for all the good it will do; he has neither men nor money to make war.
Sound, sound alarum! we will rush on them. / Now for the honour of the forlorn French! / Him I forgive my death that killeth me / When he sees me go back one foot or flee.
Sound the alarm! We'll charge them. Now for the honour of the desperate French! I forgive any man who kills me if he sees me take one step back or run.
Who ever saw the like? what men have I! / Dogs! cowards! dastards! I would ne'er have fled, / But that they left me 'midst my enemies.
Who ever saw anything like it? What men I have! Dogs! Cowards! Sneaks! I would never have run away if they hadn't left me surrounded by enemies.
Salisbury is a desperate homicide; / He fighteth as one weary of his life. / The other lords, like lions wanting food, / Do rush upon us as their hungry prey.
Salisbury is a reckless killer; he fights like a man tired of life. The other lords, like starving lions, rush at us as if we were their prey.

Froissart, a countryman of ours, records, / England all Olivers and Rowlands bred / During the time Edward the Third did reign. / More truly now may this be verified; / For none but Samsons and Goliases / It sendeth forth to skirmish. One to ten! / Lean raw-bon'd rascals! who would e'er suppose / They had such courage and audacity?

Froissart, a Frenchman, writes that in Edward the Third's reign England bred nothing but heroes like Oliver and Roland. That can be said even more truly now, for it sends out nothing but Samsons and Goliaths to fight. One against ten! Thin, bony wretches! Who would have thought they had such courage and daring?

Let's leave this town; for they are hare-brain'd slaves, / And hunger will enforce them to be more eager: / Of old I know them; rather with their teeth / The walls they'll tear down than forsake the siege.
Let's leave this town, for they are wild, reckless men, and hunger will make them fiercer. I know them of old: they'll tear down the walls with their teeth rather than give up the siege.
I think by some odd gimmors or device / Their arms are set like clocks, still to strike on; / Else ne'er could they hold out so as they do. / By my consent, we'll even let them alone.
I think their arms are set by some odd gears or device, like clocks, to keep on striking; otherwise they could never hold out as they do. If you ask me, we'll just leave them alone.
Where's the Prince Dauphin? I have news for him.
Where's the Prince Dauphin? I have news for him.
Bastard of Orleans, thrice welcome to us.
Bastard of Orleans, three times welcome.

Methinks your looks are sad, your cheer appall'd: / Hath the late overthrow wrought this offence? / Be not dismay'd, for succour is at hand: / A holy maid hither with me I bring, / Which by a vision sent to her from heaven / Ordained is to raise this tedious siege, / And drive the English forth the bounds of France. / The spirit of deep prophecy she hath, / Exceeding the nine sibyls of old Rome: / What's past and what's to come she can descry. / Speak, shall I call her in? Believe my words, / For they are certain and unfallible.

You look sad, and your faces are pale with fear. Has the recent defeat caused this? Don't lose heart, for help is near. I have brought a holy maid with me who, through a vision sent to her from heaven, has been chosen to break this long siege and drive the English out of France. She has the gift of deep prophecy, greater than the nine sibyls of ancient Rome. She can see what has happened and what is to come. Tell me, shall I call her in? Believe me, my words are true and certain.

Go, call her in. [Exit Bastard] / But first, to try her skill, / Reignier, stand thou as Dauphin in my place; / Question her proudly; let thy looks be stern: / By this means shall we sound what skill she hath.
Go, call her in. (The Bastard leaves) But first, to test her skill, Reignier, take my place as Dauphin. Question her haughtily and look stern. This way we'll find out what skill she has.
Fair maid, is 't thou wilt do these wondrous feats?
Lovely girl, are you the one who will do these wonderful deeds?

Reignier is 't thou that thinkest to beguile me? / Where is the Dauphin? Come, come from behind; / I know thee well, though never seen before. / Be not amazed, there's nothing hid from me. / In private will I talk with thee apart. / Stand back, you lords, and give us leave awhile.

Reignier, are you the one who thinks he can trick me? Where is the Dauphin? Come, come out from behind there. I know you well, though I've never seen you before. Don't be amazed; nothing is hidden from me. I will talk with you privately. Stand back, lords, and leave us alone a while.
She takes upon her bravely at first dash.
She acts boldly right from the start.

Dauphin, I am by birth a shepherd's daughter, / My wit untrain'd in any kind of art. / Heaven and our Lady gracious hath it pleased / To shine on my contemptible estate: / Lo, whilst I waited on my tender lambs / And to sun's parching heat display'd my cheeks, / God's mother deigned to appear to me, / And in a vision full of majesty / Will'd me to leave my base vocation, / And free my country from calamity: / Her aid she promised and assured success: / In complete glory she reveal'd herself; / And, whereas I was black and swart before, / With those clear rays which she infused on me / That beauty am I bless'd with which you may see. / Ask me what question thou canst possible, / And I will answer unpremeditated: / My courage try by combat, if thou dar'st, / And thou shalt find that I exceed my sex. / Resolve on this, thou shalt be fortunate, / If thou receive me for thy warlike mate.

Dauphin, I was born a shepherd's daughter, my mind untrained in any skill. Heaven and our gracious Lady have chosen to shine on my lowly state. While I was tending my young lambs, my cheeks exposed to the scorching sun, the mother of God appeared to me in a majestic vision and told me to leave my humble work and free my country from disaster. She promised her help and guaranteed success. She revealed herself in full glory, and whereas before I was dark and sunburnt, the bright rays she poured on me gave me the beauty you can see. Ask me any question you like and I'll answer without preparing. Test my courage in combat if you dare, and you'll find I go beyond what is expected of my sex. Be sure of this: you'll be lucky if you accept me as your partner in war.

Thou hast astonish'd me with thy high terms; / Only this proof I'll of thy valour make, / In single combat thou shalt buckle with me, / And if thou vanquishest, thy words are true; / Otherwise I renounce all confidence.
You have amazed me with your bold words. I'll test your courage in just one way: you will fight me in single combat. If you win, your words are true; if not, I'll reject all trust in you.

I am prepared: here is my keen-edg'd sword, / Deck'd with five flower-de-luces on each side, / The which at Touraine, in Saint Katharine's church-yard, / Out of a great deal of old iron I chose forth.
I am ready. Here is my sharp sword, decorated with five fleurs-de-lis on each side, which I chose out of a great heap of old iron in Saint Katharine's churchyard in Touraine.
Then come, o' God's name; I fear no woman.
Then come on, in God's name. I'm not afraid of any woman.
And while I live, I'll ne'er fly from a man.
And as long as I live, I'll never run from a man.
Stay, stay thy hands; thou art an Amazon, / And fightest with the sword of Deborah.
Stop, stop! You are an Amazon, and you fight with the sword of Deborah.
Christ's Mother helps me, else I were too weak.
Christ's mother helps me, or I would be too weak.

Whoe'er helps thee, 'tis thou that must help me: / Impatiently I burn with thy desire; / My heart and hands thou hast at once subdued. / Excellent Pucelle, if thy name be so, / Let me thy servant and not sovereign be: / 'Tis the French Dauphin sueth to thee thus.

Whoever helps you, it's you who must help me. I burn impatiently with desire for you; you have conquered my heart and my hands at once. Excellent Pucelle, if that's your name, let me be your servant, not your king. It's the French Dauphin who begs you like this.
I must not yield to any rites of love, / For my profession's sacred from above: / When I have chased all thy foes from hence, / Then will I think upon a recompense.
I must not give way to any love-making, for my calling is holy, from heaven. When I have chased all your enemies away, then I'll think about a reward.
Meantime look gracious on thy prostrate thrall.
Meanwhile, look kindly on your humbled slave.
My lord, methinks, is very long in talk.
My lord is talking for a very long time, I think.
Doubtless he shrives this woman to her smock; / Else ne'er could he so long protract his speech.
No doubt he's hearing this woman's confession down to her underwear; otherwise he couldn't drag out his talk so long.
Shall we disturb him, since he keeps no mean?
Shall we interrupt him, since he doesn't know when to stop?
He may mean more than we poor men do know: / These women are shrewd tempters with their tongues.
He may mean more than we poor men know. These women are clever temptresses with their tongues.
My lord, where are you? what devise you on? / Shall we give over Orleans, or no?
My lord, what are you up to? What are you planning? Shall we give up Orleans or not?
Why, no, I say; distrustful recreants! / Fight till the last gasp; I will be your guard.
No, I say! You doubting cowards! Fight to the last breath; I will protect you.
What she says I'll confirm: we'll fight it out:
I'll back up what she says: we'll fight it out.

Assign'd am I to be the English scourge. / This night the siege assuredly I'll raise: / Expect Saint Martin's summer, halcyon days, / Since I have entered into these wars. / Glory is like a circle in the water, / Which never ceaseth to enlarge itself / Till by broad spreading it disperse to nought. / With Henry's death the English circle ends; / Dispersed are the glories it included. / Now am I like that proud insulting ship / Which Caesar and his fortune bare at once.

I am appointed to be the scourge of the English. Tonight I will certainly break the siege. Expect a late summer of calm, peaceful days now that I have joined these wars. Glory is like a ripple in water, which keeps spreading wider until it spreads so far it vanishes. With Henry's death the English ripple ends; the glories it held are scattered. Now I am like that proud, triumphant ship that carried Caesar and his good fortune together.

Was Mahomet inspired with a dove? / Thou with an eagle art inspired then. / Helen, the mother of great Constantine, / Nor yet Saint Philip's daughters, were like thee. / Bright star of Venus, fall'n down on the earth, / How may I reverently worship thee enough?

Was Mahomet inspired by a dove? Then you are inspired by an eagle. Neither Helen, the mother of great Constantine, nor Saint Philip's daughters were your equal. Bright star of Venus fallen to earth, how can I worship you enough?
Leave off delays, and let us raise the siege.
Stop delaying, and let's break the siege.
Woman, do what thou canst to save our honors; / Drive them from Orleans and be immortalized.
Woman, do what you can to save our honour. Drive them from Orleans and be famous forever.
Presently we'll try: come, let's away about it: / No prophet will I trust, if she prove false.
We'll try at once. Come, let's get on with it. I'll trust no prophet again if she proves false.
I am come to survey the Tower this day: / Since Henry's death, I fear, there is conveyance. / Where be these warders that they wait not here? / Open the gates; 'tis Gloucester that calls.
I've come to inspect the Tower today. Since Henry's death I'm afraid there's been some theft. Where are the guards? Why aren't they on duty? Open the gates; it's Gloucester calling.
[Within] Who's there that knocks so imperiously?
It is the noble Duke of Gloucester.
It's the noble Duke of Gloucester.
[Within] Whoe'er he be, you may not be let in.
(From inside) Whoever he is, you can't come in.
Villains, answer you so the lord protector?
You villains, is that how you answer the Lord Protector?
[Within] The Lord protect him! so we answer him: / We do no otherwise than we are will'd.
(From inside) The Lord protect him! That's our answer. We're only doing as we're told.
Who willed you? or whose will stands but mine? / There's none protector of the realm but I. / Break up the gates, I'll be your warrantize: / Shall I be flouted thus by dunghill grooms?
Who told you? Whose orders count except mine? There's no protector of the kingdom but me. Break down the gates; I'll take responsibility. Am I to be mocked like this by filthy servants?
What noise is this? what traitors have we here?
What's this noise? What traitors are these?
Lieutenant, is it you whose voice I hear? / Open the gates; here's Gloucester that would enter.
Lieutenant, is that your voice? Open the gates; it's Gloucester who wants to come in.
Have patience, noble duke; I may not open; / The Cardinal of Winchester forbids: / From him I have express commandment / That thou nor none of thine shall be let in.
Be patient, noble Duke; I can't open them. The Cardinal of Winchester forbids it. He has given me strict orders that neither you nor any of your men are to be let in.

Faint-hearted Woodvile, prizest him 'fore me? / Arrogant Winchester, that haughty prelate / Whom Henry, our late sovereign, ne'er could brook? / Thou art no friend to God or to the King. / Open the gates, or I'll shut thee out shortly.

Cowardly Woodvile, do you value him above me? Arrogant Winchester, that proud churchman whom Henry, our late king, could never stand? You are no friend to God or the King. Open the gates, or I'll soon throw you out.
Open the gates unto the lord protector, / Or we'll burst them open, if that you come not quickly.
Open the gates to the Lord Protector, or we'll burst them open if you don't come quickly.
How now, ambitious Humphry! what means this?
What now, ambitious Humphrey! What does this mean?
Peel'd priest, dost thou command me to be shut out?
Bald-headed priest, are you ordering me to be shut out?
I do, thou most usurping proditor, / And not protector, of the king or realm.
I am, you complete traitor, the usurper, not the protector, of the King and kingdom.

Stand back, thou manifest conspirator, / Thou that contrivedst to murder our dead lord; / Thou that givest whores indulgences to sin: / I'll canvass thee in thy broad cardinal's hat, / If thou proceed in this thy insolence.
Stand back, you obvious conspirator, you who plotted to murder our dead king, you who sell pardons to whores so they can sin! I'll toss you in your broad cardinal's hat if you keep up this insolence.
Nay, stand thou back; I will not budge a foot: / This be Damascus, be thou cursed Cain, / To slay thy brother Abel, if thou wilt.
No, you stand back; I won't move an inch. Let this be Damascus, where Cain killed Abel; be cursed Cain and kill your brother if you want.
I will not slay thee, but I'll drive thee back: / Thy scarlet robes as a child's bearing-cloth / I'll use to carry thee out of this place.
I won't kill you, but I'll drive you back. I'll use your scarlet robes like a baby's christening blanket to carry you out of here.
Do what thou darest; I beard thee to thy face.
Do your worst; I defy you to your face.

What! am I dared and bearded to my face? / Draw, men, for all this privileged place; / Blue coats to tawny coats. Priest, beware your beard; / I mean to tug it and to cuff you soundly: / Under my feet I stamp thy cardinal's hat: / In spite of pope or dignities of church, / Here by the cheeks I'll drag thee up and down.

What! Am I defied and insulted to my face? Draw, men, even though this is protected ground. Blue coats against tawny coats! Priest, watch your beard; I mean to pull it and give you a good beating. I'll stamp your cardinal's hat under my feet. In spite of the Pope or any church dignitaries, I'll drag you up and down by the cheeks.
Gloucester, thou wilt answer this before the / pope.
Gloucester, you'll answer to the Pope for this.
Winchester goose, I cry, a rope! a rope! / Now beat them hence; why do you let them stay? / Thee I'll chase hence, thou wolf in sheep's array. / Out, tawny coats! out, scarlet hypocrite!
Winchester goose! I call for a rope, a rope! Now drive them away; why do you let them stay? I'll chase you away, you wolf in sheep's clothing. Out, tawny coats! Out, scarlet hypocrite!
Fie, lords! that you, being supreme magistrates, / Thus contumeliously should break the peace!
Shame, lords! You are the highest officers of the state, and you insult the law by breaking the peace like this!
Peace, mayor! thou know'st little of my wrongs: / Here's Beaufort, that regards nor God nor king, / Hath here distrain'd the Tower to his use.
Quiet, Mayor! You know little of the wrongs done to me. Here's Beaufort, who respects neither God nor King, and has seized the Tower for his own use.

Here's Gloucester, a foe to citizens, / One that still motions war and never peace, / O'ercharging your free purses with large fines, / That seeks to overthrow religion, / Because he is protector of the realm, / And would have armour here out of the Tower, / To crown himself king and suppress the prince.

Here's Gloucester, an enemy to citizens, a man who always proposes war and never peace, who loads your purses with heavy taxes, who wants to overthrow the Church because he is Protector of the kingdom, and who wants weapons out of the Tower to crown himself king and push aside the Prince.
I will not answer thee with words, but blows.
I won't answer you with words, but with blows.
Nought rests for me in this tumultuous strife / But to make open proclamation: / Come, officer; as loud as e'er thou canst: / Cry.
There's nothing for me to do in this violent quarrel but make a public proclamation. Come, officer, as loud as you can: cry it out.

All manner of men assembled here in arms / this day against God's peace and the king's, we charge / and command you, in his highness' name, to repair to / your several dwelling-places; and not to wear, handle, or / use any sword, weapon, or dagger, henceforward, upon / pain of death.

All men gathered here in arms today against the peace of God and the King: we order and command you, in his Highness's name, to go back to your homes and not to wear, handle or use any sword, weapon or dagger from now on, on pain of death.
Cardinal, I'll be no breaker of the law; / But we shall meet, and break our minds at large.
Cardinal, I won't break the law; but we'll meet and speak our minds in full.
Gloucester, we will meet; to thy cost, be sure; / Thy heart-blood I will have for this day's work.
Gloucester, we'll meet, and it will cost you, be sure. I'll have your heart's blood for this day's work.
I'll call for clubs, if you will not away. / This Cardinal's more haughty than the devil.
I'll call for the constables with their clubs if you won't leave. This Cardinal is more arrogant than the devil.
Mayor, farewell: thou dost but what thou mayst.
Mayor, goodbye. You're only doing what you must.
Abominable Gloucester, guard thy head; / For I intend to have it ere long.
Hateful Gloucester, guard your head, for I intend to have it before long.
See the coast clear'd, and then we will depart. / Good God, these nobles should such stomachs bear! / I myself fight not once in forty year.
Make sure the area is clear, and then we'll leave. Good God, how these nobles carry grudges! I don't fight once in forty years.
Sirrah, thou know'st how Orleans is besieged, / And how the English have the suburbs won.
Boy, you know how Orleans is under siege and how the English have captured the suburbs.
Father, I know; and oft have shot at them, / Howe'er unfortunate I miss'd my aim.
Father, I know, and I've often shot at them, though unluckily I missed.

But now thou shalt not. Be thou ruled by me: / Chief master-gunner am I of this town; / Something I must do to procure me grace. / The prince's espials have informed me / How the English, in the suburbs close intrench'd, / Wont through a secret grate of iron bars / In yonder tower to overpeer the city, / And thence discover how with most advantage / They may vex us with shot or with assault. / To intercept this inconvenience, / A piece of ordnance 'gainst it I have placed; / And even these three days have I watch'd, / If I could see them. / Now do thou watch, for I can stay no longer. / If thou spy'st any, run and bring me word; / And thou shalt find me at the governor's.

But now you won't miss. Do as I say. I'm the chief gunner of this town; I must do something to win favour. The Prince's spies have told me that the English, dug in close in the suburbs, are in the habit of looking over the city through a secret iron grating in that tower, to work out how best to attack us with gunfire or assault. To stop this nuisance, I've aimed a cannon at it, and for three days now I've watched to see if I could spot them. Now you keep watch, for I can't stay any longer. If you see anyone, run and tell me; you'll find me at the governor's.
Father, I warrant you; take you no care; / I'll never trouble you, if I may spy them.
Father, I promise you; don't worry. I won't bother you if I can spot them.
Talbot, my life, my joy, again return'd! / How wert thou handled being prisoner? / Or by what means got'st thou to be releas'd? / Discourse, I prithee, on this turret's top.
Talbot, my life, my joy, back again! How were you treated as a prisoner? How did you manage to get released? Tell me about it, please, here on this turret.

The Duke of Bedford had a prisoner / Call'd the brave Lord Ponton de Santrailles; / For him was I exchanged and ransomed. / But with a baser man of arms by far / Once in contempt they would have barter'd me: / Which I disdaining scorn'd, and craved death / Rather than I would be so vile-esteem'd. / In fine, redeem'd I was as I desired. / But, O! the treacherous Fastolfe wounds my heart, / Whom with my bare fists I would execute, / If I now had him brought into my power.

The Duke of Bedford had a prisoner called the brave Lord Ponton de Santrailles; I was exchanged and ransomed for him. Once, to insult me, they wanted to swap me for a far lower-ranking soldier, which I scornfully refused, asking for death rather than be valued so cheaply. In the end I was released as I wanted. But oh, treacherous Fastolfe wounds my heart! I would kill him with my bare hands if I had him in my power now.
Yet tell'st thou not how thou wert entertain'd.
You still haven't told me how you were treated.

With scoffs and scorns and contumelious taunts. / In open market-place produced they me, / To be a public spectacle to all: / Here, said they, is the terror of the French, / The scarecrow that affrights our children so. / Then broke I from the officers that led me, / And with my nails digg'd stones out of the ground / To hurl at the beholders of my shame; / My grisly countenance made others fly; / None durst come near for fear of sudden death. / In iron walls they deem'd me not secure; / So great fear of my name 'mongst them was spread / That they supposed I could rend bars of steel, / And spurn in pieces posts of adamant: / Wherefore a guard of chosen shot I had, / That walk'd about me every minute while; / And if I did but stir out of my bed, / Ready they were to shoot me to the heart.

With mockery, scorn and insulting taunts. They put me on show in the open market-place as a public spectacle for everyone. "Here," they said, "is the terror of the French, the bogeyman who frightens our children." Then I broke away from the officers who led me and dug stones out of the ground with my nails to throw at the people watching my shame. My grim face made others run; nobody dared come near for fear of instant death. They didn't think I was safe even behind iron walls; the fear of my name spread so far among them that they believed I could break steel bars and kick unbreakable posts to pieces. So I had a guard of picked marksmen who walked around me every minute, and if I so much as got out of bed they were ready to shoot me through the heart.

I grieve to hear what torments you endured, / But we will be revenged sufficiently. / Now it is supper-time in Orleans: / Here, through this grate, I count each one, / And view the Frenchmen how they fortify: / Let us look in; the sight will much delight thee. / Sir Thomas Gargrave and Sir William Glansdale, / Let me have your express opinions / Where is best place to make our battery next.

I'm sorry to hear what torments you suffered, but we'll get revenge enough. It's supper time in Orleans now. Through this grating I can count each one of them and see how the French are fortifying. Let's look in; the sight will cheer you. Sir Thomas Gargrave and Sir William Glansdale, give me your opinions on the best place for our next bombardment.
I think, at the north gate; for there stand lords.
I think the north gate, for the lords are there.
And I, here, at the bulwark of the bridge.
And I think here, at the fortification on the bridge.
For aught I see, this city must be famish'd, / Or with light skirmishes enfeebled.
As far as I can see, this city must be starved out or worn down with small attacks.
O Lord, have mercy on us, wretched sinners!
O Lord, have mercy on us, miserable sinners!
O Lord, have mercy on me, woful man!
O Lord, have mercy on me, a wretched man!

What chance is this that suddenly hath cross'd us? / Speak, Salisbury: at least, if thou canst speak: / How farest thou, mirror of all martial men? / One of thy eyes and thy cheek's side struck off! / Accursed tower! accursed fatal hand / That hath contrived this woful tragedy! / In thirteen battles Salisbury o'ercame; / Henry the Fifth he first train'd to the wars; / Whilst any trump did sound, or drum struck up, / His sword did ne'er leave striking in the field. / Yet liv'st thou, Salisbury? though thy speech doth fail, / One eye thou hast, to look to heaven for grace: / The sun with one eye vieweth all the world. / Heaven, be thou gracious to none alive, / If Salisbury wants mercy at thy hands! / Bear hence his body; I will help to bury it, / Sir Thomas Gargrave, hast thou any life? / Speak unto Talbot; nay, look up to him. / Salisbury, cheer thy spirit with this comfort, / Thou shalt not die whiles— / He beckons with his hand and smiles on me, / As who should say 'When I am dead and gone, / Remember to avenge me on the French.' / Plantagenet, I will; and like thee, Nero, / Play on the lute, beholding the towns burn; / Wretched shall France be only in thy name.

What disaster is this that has suddenly struck us? Speak, Salisbury, if you can speak at all. How are you, model of all soldiers? One of your eyes and the side of your face blown off! Cursed tower! Cursed deadly hand that caused this sad tragedy! Salisbury won thirteen battles; he trained Henry the Fifth in war. While any trumpet sounded or drum beat, his sword never stopped striking on the battlefield. Are you still alive, Salisbury? Though your voice fails, you have one eye left to look to heaven for mercy. The sun sees the whole world with one eye. Heaven, show mercy to no one alive if you deny it to Salisbury! Carry his body away; I'll help bury it. Sir Thomas Gargrave, are you alive? Speak to Talbot; no, look up at him. Salisbury, take comfort in this: you won't die while— He beckons and smiles at me, as if to say, "When I am dead and gone, remember to take revenge on the French for me." Plantagenet, I will; and like Nero I'll play the lute while watching the towns burn. Your name alone will bring misery to France.
What stir is this? what tumult's in the heavens? / Whence cometh this alarum and the noise?
What's this commotion? What uproar is this in the skies? Where is this alarm and noise coming from?
My lord, my lord, the French have gather'd head: / The Dauphin, with one Joan la Pucelle join'd, / A holy prophetess new risen up, / Is come with a great power to raise the siege.
My lord, my lord, the French have gathered their forces. The Dauphin, joined by one Joan la Pucelle, a holy prophetess who has newly appeared, has come with a great army to break the siege.

Hear, hear how dying Salisbury doth groan! / It irks his heart he cannot be revenged. / Frenchmen, I'll be a Salisbury to you: / Pucelle or puzzel, dolphin or dogfish, / Your hearts I'll stamp out with my horse's heels, / And make a quagmire of your mingled brains. / Convey me Salisbury into his tent, / And then we'll try what these dastard Frenchmen dare.

Listen, listen how dying Salisbury groans! It pains his heart that he can't take revenge. Frenchmen, I'll be a Salisbury to you. Pucelle or slut, dauphin or dogfish, I'll stamp out your hearts with my horse's hooves and turn your mixed-up brains into a swamp. Carry Salisbury to his tent for me, and then we'll see what these cowardly Frenchmen dare to do.
Where is my strength, my valor, and my force? / Our English troops retire, I cannot stay them: / A woman clad in armour chaseth them.
Where is my strength, my courage and my force? Our English troops are retreating; I can't stop them. A woman dressed in armour is chasing them.
Here, here she comes. I'll have a bout with thee; / Devil or devil's dam, I'll conjure thee: / Blood will I draw on thee, thou art a witch, / And straightway give thy soul to him thou servest.
Here, here she comes. I'll have a fight with you. Devil or devil's mother, I'll drive the spirit out of you. I'll draw your blood, you witch, and send your soul straight to the master you serve.
Come, come, 'tis only I that must disgrace thee.
Come on, come on; I'm the one who will shame you.
Heavens, can you suffer hell so to prevail? / My breast I'll burst with straining of my courage, / And from my shoulders crack my arms asunder, / But I will chastise this high-minded strumpet.
Heavens, can you let hell win like this? I'll burst my chest straining my courage and crack my arms from my shoulders, but I'll punish this arrogant whore.
Talbot, farewell; thy hour is not yet come: / I must go victual Orleans forthwith.
Talbot, goodbye; your time hasn't come yet. I must go and bring supplies into Orleans at once.
O'ertake me, if thou canst; I scorn thy strength. / Go, go, cheer up thy hungry-starved men; / Help Salisbury to make his testament: / This day is ours, as many more shall be.
Catch me if you can; I scorn your strength. Go, go and cheer up your starving men. Help Salisbury make his will. This day is ours, and many more will be.

My thoughts are whirled like a potter's wheel; / I know not where I am, nor what I do; / A witch, by fear, not force, like Hannibal, / Drives back our troops and conquers as she lists. / So bees with smoke and doves with noisome stench / Are from their hives and houses driven away. / They call'd us for our fierceness English dogs; / Now, like to whelps, we crying run away.

My thoughts are spinning like a potter's wheel; I don't know where I am or what I'm doing. A witch, like Hannibal, drives back our troops by fear, not force, and wins as she pleases. That's how bees are driven from their hives by smoke and doves from their dovecotes by foul smells. They used to call us English dogs because we were so fierce; now we run away whimpering like puppies.

Hark, countrymen! either renew the fight, / Or tear the lions out of England's coat; / Renounce your soil, give sheep in lions' stead: / Sheep run not half so treacherous from the wolf, / Or horse or oxen from the leopard, / As you fly from your oft-subdued slaves.

Listen, countrymen! Either start fighting again or tear the lions off England's coat of arms. Give up your country and put sheep in place of lions. Sheep don't run from the wolf, or horses and oxen from the leopard, half as disloyally as you run from the slaves you have so often beaten.

It will not be: retire into your trenches: / You all consented unto Salisbury's death, / For none would strike a stroke in his revenge. / Pucelle is ent'red into Orleans, / In spite of us or aught that we could do. / O, would I were to die with Salisbury! / The shame hereof will make me hide my head.

It's no use. Retreat to your trenches. You all agreed to Salisbury's death, since none of you would strike a blow to avenge him. Pucelle has got into Orleans in spite of us and everything we could do. Oh, I wish I had died with Salisbury! The shame of this will make me hide my face.
Advance our waving colours on the walls; / Rescued is Orleans from the English: / Thus Joan la Pucelle hath perform'd her word.
Raise our waving flags on the walls. Orleans is rescued from the English. So Joan la Pucelle has kept her word.

Divinest creature, Astraea's daughter, / How shall I honour thee for this success? / Thy promises are like Adonis' gardens / That one day bloom'd and fruitful were the next. / France, triumph in thy glorious prophetess! / Recover'd is the town of Orleans. / More blessed hap did ne'er befall our state.

Most divine creature, daughter of Astraea, goddess of justice, how shall I honour you for this success? Your promises are like the gardens of Adonis, which flowered one day and bore fruit the next. France, rejoice in your glorious prophetess! The town of Orleans is won back. Nothing more fortunate ever happened to our country.
Why ring not out the bells aloud throughout the town? / Dauphin, command the citizens make bonfires / And feast and banquet in the open streets, / To celebrate the joy that God hath given us.
Why aren't the bells ringing out loud all through the town? Dauphin, order the citizens to light bonfires and feast and celebrate in the open streets to mark the joy God has given us.
All France will be replete with mirth and joy, / When they shall hear how we have play'd the men.
All France will be full of happiness and joy when they hear how bravely we have fought.

'Tis Joan, not we, by whom the day is won; / For which I will divide my crown with her; / And all the priests and friars in my realm / Shall in procession sing her endless praise. / A statelier pyramis to her I'll rear / Than Rhodope's of Memphis ever was; / In memory of her when she is dead, / Her ashes, in an urn more precious / Than the rich-jewel'd coffer of Darius, / Transported shall be at high festivals / Before the kings and queens of France. / No longer on Saint Denis will we cry, / But Joan la Pucelle shall be France's saint. / Come in, and let us banquet royally / After this golden day of victory.

It's Joan, not us, who won the day, and for that I'll share my crown with her, and all the priests and friars in my kingdom will sing her praises forever in processions. I'll build her a grander pyramid than Rhodope's in Memphis. In memory of her, when she is dead, her ashes will be carried at great festivals before the kings and queens of France in an urn more precious than the jewelled chest of Darius. We'll no longer pray to Saint Denis; Joan la Pucelle will be the saint of France. Come in, and let's feast like kings after this golden day of victory.
Sirs, take your places and be vigilant: / If any noise or soldier you perceive / Near to the walls, by some apparent sign / Let us have knowledge at the court of guard.
Men, take your places and stay alert. If you notice any noise or soldier near the walls, let us know at the guardhouse with some clear signal.
Sergeant, you shall. [Exit Sergeant] / Thus are poor servitors, / When others sleep upon their quiet beds, / Constrain'd to watch in darkness, rain and cold.
Sergeant, we will. (The Sergeant leaves) This is how poor servants have to keep watch in darkness, rain and cold while others sleep in their quiet beds.

Lord Regent, and redoubted Burgundy, / By whose approach the regions of Artois, / Wallon and Picardy are friends to us, / This happy night the Frenchmen are secure, / Having all day caroused and banqueted: / Embrace we then this opportunity, / As fitting best to quittance their deceit / Contriv'd by art and baleful sorcery.

Lord Regent, and honoured Burgundy, whose coming has made the regions of Artois, Walloon Flanders and Picardy our friends: tonight the French feel safe after feasting and drinking all day. Let's take this chance, as the best way to pay back their trickery, plotted with magic and evil sorcery.
Coward of France, how much he wrongs his fame, / Despairing of his own arm's fortitude, / To join with witches and the help of hell!
The coward of France! How he damages his reputation, giving up on the strength of his own arm and joining with witches and the help of hell!
Traitors have never other company. / But what 's that Pucelle whom they term so pure?
Traitors never keep any other company. But who is this Pucelle they call so pure?
A maid! and be so martial!
Pray God she prove not masculine ere long, / If underneath the standard of the French / She carry armour as she hath begun.
Pray God she doesn't turn out to be with a man's child soon, if she keeps bearing arms under the French flag as she has started.
Well, let them practice and converse with spirits: / God is our fortress, in whose conquering name / Let us resolve to scale their flinty bulwarks.
Well, let them plot and deal with spirits. God is our fortress, and in his conquering name let's be determined to climb their stone walls.
Ascend, brave Talbot; we will follow thee.
Climb, brave Talbot; we'll follow you.
Not all together: better far, I guess, / That we do make our entrance several ways; / That, if it chance the one of us do fail, / The other yet may rise against their force.
Not all together. Much better, I think, that we break in at different places, so that if one of us happens to fail, the other can still rise against their forces.
Agreed. I'll go to that corner.
And here will Talbot mount, or make his grave. / Now, Salisbury, for thee, and for the right / Of English Henry, shall this night appear / How much in duty I am bound to both.
And here Talbot will climb, or make his grave here. Now, Salisbury, for you and for the rights of English Henry, tonight will show how much I owe to both of you.
Arm! arm! the enemy doth make assault!
To arms! To arms! The enemy is attacking!
How now, my lords! what, all unready so?
What's this, my lords? What, all half-dressed?
Unready! aye, and glad we 'scap'd so well.
Half-dressed! Yes, and glad we escaped so well.
'Twas time, I trow, to wake and leave our beds, / Hearing alarums at our chamber-doors.
It was time, I think, to wake up and leave our beds, hearing alarms at our bedroom doors.
Of all exploits since first I follow'd arms, / Ne'er heard I of a warlike enterprise / More venturous or desperate than this.
Of all the exploits I've heard of since I first became a soldier, I never heard of a military venture more daring or desperate than this.
I think this Talbot be a fiend of hell.
I think this Talbot is a devil from hell.
If not of hell, the heavens, sure, favor him.
If not from hell, then the heavens must surely favour him.
Here cometh Charles: I marvel how he sped.
Here comes Charles. I wonder how he got on.
Tut, holy Joan was his defensive guard.
Pooh, holy Joan was protecting him.
Is this thy cunning, thou deceitful dame? / Didst thou at first, to flatter us withal, / Make us partakers of a little gain, / That now our loss might be ten times so much?
Is this your skill, you deceitful woman? Did you first give us a little gain, to flatter us, so that our loss now might be ten times as great?

Wherefore is Charles impatient with his friend? / At all times will you have my power alike? / Sleeping or waking must I still prevail, / Or will you blame and lay the fault on me? / Improvident soldiers! had your watch been good, / This sudden mischief never could have fall'n.

Why is Charles impatient with his friend? Do you expect my power to be the same at all times? Must I always win, asleep or awake, or else you'll blame me and put the fault on me? Careless soldiers! If you had kept good watch, this sudden disaster could never have happened.
Duke of Alencon, this was your default, / That, being captain of the watch to-night, / Did look no better to that weighty charge.
Duke of Alencon, this was your fault: you were captain of the watch tonight and didn't look after that important duty better.
Had all your quarters been as safely kept / As that whereof I had the government, / We had not been thus shamefully surprised.
If all your areas had been as well guarded as the one I was in charge of, we wouldn't have been so shamefully surprised.
And so was mine, my lord.
And so was mine, my lord.

And, for myself, most part of all this night, / Within her quarter and mine own precinct / I was employ'd in passing to and fro, / About relieving of the sentinels: / Then how or which way should they first break in?
And as for me, I spent most of the night going back and forth within her area and my own, relieving the sentries. So how, or which way, could they have broken in first?

Question, my lords, no further of the case, / How or which way: 'tis sure they found some place / But weakly guarded, where the breach was made. / And now there rests no other shift but this; / To gather our soldiers, scatter'd and dispersed, / And lay new platforms to endamage them.

Don't question any further, my lords, how or which way. It's certain they found some weakly guarded place and broke in there. And now there's nothing left to do but gather our scattered soldiers and make new plans to damage them.
I'll be so bold to take what they have left. / The cry of Talbot serves me for a sword; / For I have loaden me with many spoils, / Using no other weapon but his name.
I'll make so bold as to take what they've left. The cry of "Talbot" is as good as a sword to me, for I've loaded myself with loot using no weapon but his name.
The day begins to break, and night is fled, / Whose pitchy mantle over-veil'd the earth. / Here sound retreat, and cease our hot pursuit.
Day is beginning to break and night has fled, whose pitch-black cloak covered the earth. Sound the retreat here and stop our fierce pursuit.

Bring forth the body of old Salisbury, / And here advance it in the market-place, / The middle centre of this cursed town. / Now have I paid my vow unto his soul; / For every drop of blood was drawn from him / There hath at least five Frenchmen died to-night. / And that hereafter ages may behold / What ruin happen'd in revenge of him, / Within their chiefest temple I'll erect / A tomb, wherein his corpse shall be interr'd; / Upon the which, that every one may read, / Shall be engraved the sack of Orleans, / The treacherous manner of his mournful death / And what a terror he had been to France. / But, lords, in all our bloody massacre, / I muse we met not with the Dauphin's grace, / His new-come champion, virtuous Joan of Arc, / Nor any of his false confederates.

Bring out the body of old Salisbury and set it up here in the market-place, the very centre of this cursed town. Now I have kept my vow to his soul: for every drop of blood drawn from him, at least five Frenchmen have died tonight. And so that future ages may see what destruction happened to avenge him, I'll build a tomb in their main church where his body will be buried, and on it, for everyone to read, will be carved the sack of Orleans, the treacherous way he died and what a terror he had been to France. But, lords, in all our bloody slaughter I'm surprised we didn't meet his Grace the Dauphin, his new champion, the virtuous Joan of Arc, or any of his treacherous allies.
'Tis thought, Lord Talbot, when the fight began, / Rous'd on the sudden from their drowsy beds, / They did amongst the troops of armed men / Leap o'er the walls for refuge in the field.
It's thought, Lord Talbot, that when the fighting started, woken suddenly from their sleepy beds, they jumped over the walls among the soldiers to take refuge in the fields.

Myself, as far as I could well discern / For smoke and dusky vapors of the night, / Am sure I scared the Dauphin and his trull, / When arm in arm they both came swiftly running, / Like to a pair of loving turtle-doves / That could not live asunder day or night. / After that things are set in order here, / We'll follow them with all the power we have.

As far as I could make out through the smoke and the dark mists of the night, I'm sure I frightened off the Dauphin and his whore as they came running arm in arm, like a pair of loving turtle-doves who couldn't live apart day or night. Once things are in order here, we'll follow them with all the forces we have.
All hail, my lords! Which of this princely train / Call ye the warlike Talbot, for his acts / So much applauded through the realm of France?
Greetings, my lords! Which of this princely company is the warlike Talbot, whose deeds are so praised throughout France?
Here is the Talbot: who would speak with him?
Here is Talbot. Who wants to speak to him?

The virtuous lady, Countess of Auvergne, / With modesty admiring thy renown, / By me entreats, great lord, thou wouldst vouchsafe / To visit her poor castle where she lies, / That she may boast she hath beheld the man / Whose glory fills the world with loud report.

The virtuous lady, the Countess of Auvergne, modestly admiring your fame, begs you through me, great lord, to be so kind as to visit her humble castle where she lives, so that she can boast she has seen the man whose glory fills the world with loud praise.
Is it even so? Nay, then I see our wars / Will turn into a peaceful comic sport, / When ladies crave to be encount'red with. / You may not, my lord, despise her gentle suit.
Is that so? Well then, I see our wars will turn into a peaceful comedy when ladies ask to be met in combat. You can't turn down her gentle request, my lord.

Ne'er trust me then; for when a world of men / Could not prevail with all their oratory, / Yet hath a woman's kindness over-ruled: / And therefore tell her I return great thanks, / And in submission will attend on her. / Will not your honors bear me company?

Never trust me if I do. When a world of men couldn't win me over with all their eloquence, a woman's kindness has. So tell her I give her many thanks and will humbly visit her. Will your lordships come with me?
No, truly; it is more than manners will: / And I have heard it said, unbidden guests / Are often welcomest when they are gone.
No, really; that would be more than good manners allow. And I've heard it said that uninvited guests are often most welcome when they've gone.
Well then, alone, since there 's no remedy, / I mean to prove this lady's courtesy. / Come hither, Captain. [Whispers] You perceive my mind?
Well then, I'll go alone, since there's no help for it, to test this lady's courtesy. Come here, Captain. (Whispering) You understand what I want?
I do, my lord, and mean accordingly.
I do, my lord, and I'll act on it.
Porter, remember what I gave in charge; / And when you have done so, bring the keys to me.
Porter, remember what I told you to do, and when you've done it, bring the keys to me.

The plot is laid: if all things fall out right, / I shall as famous be by this exploit / As Scythian Tomyris by Cyrus' death. / Great is the rumor of this dreadful knight, / And his achievements of no less account: / Fain would mine eyes be witness with mine ears, / To give their censure of these rare reports.

The plot is set. If everything goes right, I'll be as famous for this exploit as the Scythian queen Tomyris was for killing Cyrus. Great is the fame of this fearsome knight, and his deeds are just as great. I would like my eyes to witness what my ears have heard and judge these extraordinary reports for themselves.
Madam, / according as your ladyship desired, / By message craved, so is Lord Talbot come.
Madam, as your ladyship wished and asked by message, Lord Talbot has come.
And he is welcome. What! is this the man?
And he is welcome. What! Is this the man?

Is this the scourge of France? / Is this the Talbot, so much fear'd abroad / That with his name the mothers still their babes? / I see report is fabulous and false: / I thought I should have seen some Hercules, / A second Hector, for his grim aspect, / And large proportion of his strong-knit limbs. / Alas, this is a child, a silly dwarf! / It cannot be this weak and writhled shrimp / Should strike such terror to his enemies.

Is this the scourge of France? Is this the Talbot so feared abroad that mothers quiet their babies with his name? I see the reports are made up and false. I thought I would see some Hercules, a second Hector, with a grim face and big, powerful limbs. But this is a child, a feeble dwarf! This weak, wrinkled shrimp can't possibly strike such terror into his enemies.
Madam, I have been bold to trouble you; / But since your ladyship is not at leisure, / I'll sort some other time to visit you.
Madam, I have been bold to trouble you, but since your ladyship isn't free, I'll find some other time to visit you.
What means he now? Go ask him whither he goes.
What does he mean now? Go and ask him where he's going.
Stay, my Lord Talbot; for my lady craves / To know the cause of your abrupt departure.
Wait, my Lord Talbot, for my lady wants to know why you are leaving so suddenly.
Marry, for that she's in a wrong belief, / I go to certify her Talbot's here.
Well, since she is mistaken, I'm going to prove to her that Talbot is here.
If thou be he, then art thou prisoner.
If you are he, then you are a prisoner.

To me, blood-thirsty lord; / And for that cause I train'd thee to my house. / Long time thy shadow hath been thrall to me, / For in my gallery thy picture hangs: / But now the substance shall endure the like, / And I will chain these legs and arms of thine, / That hast by tyranny these many years / Wasted our country, slain our citizens, / And sent our sons and husbands captivate.

Mine, bloodthirsty lord, and that's why I lured you to my house. Your image has long been my prisoner, for your portrait hangs in my gallery. But now the real you will suffer the same, and I'll chain these legs and arms of yours, which have for so many years cruelly ruined our country, killed our citizens and taken our sons and husbands captive.
Laughest thou, wretch? Thy mirth shall turn to moan.
Are you laughing, wretch? Your laughter will turn to groans.
I laugh to see your ladyship so fond / To think that you have aught but Talbot's shadow / Whereon to practice your severity.
I'm laughing to see your ladyship so foolish as to think you have anything but Talbot's shadow to be cruel to.
Why, art not thou the man?
Then I have the real thing too.

No, no, I am but shadow of myself: / You are deceived, my substance is not here; / For what you see is but the smallest part / And least proportion of humanity: / I tell you, madam, were the whole frame here, / It is of such a spacious lofty pitch, / Your roof were not sufficient to contain 't.

No, no, I am only a shadow of myself. You are mistaken; my real substance is not here. What you see is only the smallest part and tiniest fraction of my being. I tell you, madam, if the whole of me were here, it is so vast and tall that your roof couldn't hold it.
This is a riddling merchant for the nonce; / He will be here, and yet he is not here: / How can these contrarieties agree?
This one's a dealer in riddles, all right. He will be here, and yet he isn't here. How can these contradictions fit together?
That will I show you presently.

How say you, madam? are you now persuaded / That Talbot is but shadow of himself? / These are his substance, sinews, arms and strength, / With which he yoketh your rebellious necks, / Razeth your cities and subverts your towns, / And in a moment makes them desolate.

What do you say, madam? Are you convinced now that Talbot is only a shadow of himself? These are his substance, his muscles, arms and strength, with which he yokes your rebellious necks, flattens your cities, overthrows your towns and in a moment leaves them in ruins.

Victorious Talbot! pardon my abuse: / I find thou art no less than fame hath bruited, / And more than may be gather'd by thy shape. / Let my presumption not provoke thy wrath; / For I am sorry that with reverence / I did not entertain thee as thou art.

Victorious Talbot! Forgive my insults. I find you are no less than fame reported, and more than your appearance suggests. Don't let my arrogance make you angry; I am sorry I did not receive you with the respect you deserve.

Be not dismay'd, fair lady; nor misconstrue / The mind of Talbot, as you did mistake / The outward composition of his body. / What you have done hath not offended me; / Nor other satisfaction do I crave, / But only, with your patience, that we may / Taste of your wine and see what cates you have; / For soldiers' stomachs always serve them well.

Don't be upset, fair lady, and don't misjudge Talbot's mind as you misjudged his outward body. What you did hasn't offended me. I ask no other compensation than that, with your permission, we may taste your wine and see what delicacies you have, for soldiers always have good appetites.
With all my heart, and think me honored / To feast so great a warrior in my house.
With all my heart, and I consider myself honoured to feast so great a warrior in my house.
Great lords and gentlemen, / what means this silence? / Dare no man answer in a case of truth?
Great lords and gentlemen, why this silence? Doesn't anyone dare answer on a matter of truth?
Within the Temple-hall we were too loud; / The garden here is more convenient.
We were too loud inside the Temple hall; the garden here is more suitable.
Then say at once if I maintain'd the truth; / Or else was wrangling Somerset in the error?
Then say straight out whether I argued the truth, or whether quarrelsome Somerset was wrong.
Faith, I have been a truant in the law, / And never yet could frame my will to it; / And therefore frame the law unto my will.
Honestly, I've played truant from the law and could never bend my will to it, so I bend the law to fit my will.
Judge you, my Lord of Warwick, then, between us.
Then you judge between us, my Lord of Warwick.

Between two hawks, which flies the higher pitch; / Between two dogs, which hath the deeper mouth; / Between two blades, which bears the better temper: / Between two horses, which doth bear him best; / Between two girls, which hath the merriest eye; / I have perhaps some shallow spirit of judgment: / But in these nice sharp quillets of the law, / Good faith, I am no wiser than a daw.

Between two hawks, which flies higher; between two dogs, which has the deeper bark; between two swords, which is better tempered; between two horses, which carries itself best; between two girls, which has the merriest eye: on these I may have some shallow judgement. But in these fine, sharp quibbles of the law, honestly, I'm no wiser than a jackdaw.
Tut, tut, here is a mannerly forbearance: / The truth appears so naked on my side / That any purblind eye may find it out.
Come, come, this is just polite dodging. The truth is so plainly on my side that a half-blind eye could see it.
And on my side it is so well apparell'd, / So clear, so shining and so evident, / That it will glimmer through a blind man's eye.
And on my side it is so well dressed, so clear, so shining and so obvious that it would shine through a blind man's eye.

Since you are tongue-tied and so loath to speak, / In dumb significants proclaim your thoughts: / Let him that is a true-born gentleman / And stands upon the honor of his birth, / If he suppose that I have pleaded truth, / From off this brier pluck a white rose with me.

Since you are tongue-tied and so unwilling to speak, declare your thoughts by silent signs. Let whoever is a true-born gentleman, proud of the honour of his birth, and thinks I have argued the truth, pick a white rose from this bush with me.
Let him that is no coward nor no flatterer, / But dare maintain the party of the truth, / Pluck a red rose from off this thorn with me.
Let whoever is no coward or flatterer, but dares to support the side of truth, pick a red rose from this thorn bush with me.
I love no colours, and without all colour / Of base insinuating flattery / I pluck this white rose with Plantagenet.
I don't like pretences, and without any colour of low, sly flattery I pick this white rose with Plantagenet.
I pluck this red rose with young Somerset, / And say withal I think he held the right.
I pick this red rose with young Somerset, and I say too that I think he was right.
Stay, lords and gentlemen, and pluck no more, / Till you conclude that he, upon whose side / The fewest roses are cropp'd from the tree / Shall yield the other in the right opinion.
Wait, lords and gentlemen, and pick no more until you agree that the one whose side has the fewest roses picked from the tree will admit the other is right.
Good Master Vernon, it is well objected: / If I have fewest, I subscribe in silence.
Good Master Vernon, that's a fair point. If I have the fewest, I'll accept it in silence.
Then for the truth and plainness of the case, / I pluck this pale and maiden blossom here, / Giving my verdict on the white rose side.
Then for the truth and plain facts of the case, I pick this pale, virgin flower here, giving my verdict on the white rose side.
Prick not your finger as you pluck it off, / Lest bleeding, you do paint the white rose red, / And fall on my side so, against your will.
Don't prick your finger as you pick it, in case you bleed and paint the white rose red, and so come over to my side against your will.
If I, my lord, for my opinion bleed, / Opinion shall be surgeon to my hurt / And keep me on the side where still I am.
If I bleed for my opinion, my lord, my opinion will be the surgeon for my wound and keep me on the side where I still am.
Well, well, come on: who else?
Well, well, come on: who else?
Unless my study and my books be false, / The argument you held was wrong in you;
Unless my study and my books are wrong, the argument you put forward was mistaken. (To Somerset)
In sign whereof I pluck a white rose too.
As a sign of which, I pick a white rose too.
Now, Somerset, where is your argument?
Now, Somerset, where is your argument?
Here in my scabbard, meditating that / Shall dye your white rose in a bloody red.
Here in my scabbard, thinking about something that will dye your white rose a bloody red.
Meantime your cheeks do counterfeit our roses; / For pale they look with fear, as witnessing / The truth on our side.
Meanwhile your cheeks are imitating our roses, for they look pale with fear, as if admitting the truth is on our side.
No, Plantagenet, / 'Tis not for fear but anger that thy cheeks / Blush for pure shame to counterfeit our roses, / And yet thy tongue will not confess thy error.
No, Plantagenet, it's not fear but anger that makes your cheeks blush with pure shame and imitate our roses; and yet your tongue won't admit your mistake.
Hath not thy rose a canker, Somerset?
Hasn't your rose got a canker-worm in it, Somerset?
Hath not thy rose a thorn, Plantagenet?
Hasn't your rose got a thorn, Plantagenet?
Ay, sharp and piercing, to maintain his truth; / Whiles thy consuming canker eats his falsehood.
Yes, sharp and piercing, to defend its truth, while your devouring canker eats away its falseness.
Well, I'll find friends to wear my bleeding roses, / That shall maintain what I have said is true, / Where false Plantagenet dare not be seen.
Well, I'll find friends to wear my bleeding roses who will defend what I have said is true, where false Plantagenet doesn't dare show his face.
Now, by this maiden blossom in my hand, / I scorn thee and thy fashion, peevish boy.
By this virgin flower in my hand, I scorn you and your kind, you silly boy.
Turn not thy scorns this way, Plantagenet.
Don't aim your scorn this way, Plantagenet.
Proud Pole, I will, and scorn both him and thee.
I will, proud Pole, and scorn both him and you.
I'll turn my part thereof into thy throat.
I'll ram my share of it back down your throat.
Away, away, good William de la Pole! / We grace the yeoman by conversing with him.
Come away, come away, good William de la Pole! We honour this commoner by talking to him.
Now, by God's will, thou wrong'st him, Somerset; / His grandfather was Lionel Duke of Clarence, / Third son to the third Edward King of England: / Spring crestless yeomen from so deep a root?
By God's will, you wrong him, Somerset. His grandfather was Lionel Duke of Clarence, third son of Edward the Third, King of England. Do commoners without coats of arms grow from such a deep root?
He bears him on the place's privilege, / Or durst not, for his craven heart, say thus.
He's relying on the protection of this place, or his cowardly heart wouldn't dare say this.

By Him that made me, I'll maintain my words / On any plot of ground in Christendom. / Was not thy father, Richard Earl of Cambridge, / For treason executed in our late king's days? / And, by his treason, stand'st not thou attainted, / Corrupted, and exempt from ancient gentry? / His trespass yet lives guilty in thy blood; / And, till thou be restored, thou art a yeoman.

By the God who made me, I'll stand by my words on any patch of ground in Christendom. Wasn't your father, Richard Earl of Cambridge, executed for treason in our late king's time? And because of his treason, aren't you attainted, your blood corrupted and stripped of your ancient noble rank? His crime still lives on as guilt in your blood, and until you are restored, you are a commoner.

My father was attached, not attainted, / Condemn'd to die for treason, but no traitor; / And that I'll prove on better men than Somerset, / Were growing time once ripen'd to my will. / For your partaker Pole and you yourself, / I'll note you in my book of memory, / To scourge you for this apprehension: / Look to it well and say you are well warn'd.

My father was arrested, not attainted; condemned to die for treason, but no traitor. And I'll prove that on better men than Somerset when time ripens to suit my purpose. As for your ally Pole and you yourself, I'll write you down in my book of memory to punish you for this idea. Watch out, and remember you've been warned.
Ay, thou shalt find us ready for thee still; / And know us by these colors for thy foes, / For these my friends in spite of thee shall wear.
Yes, you'll find us always ready for you, and you'll know us as your enemies by these colours, which my friends will wear in spite of you.

And, by my soul, this pale and angry rose, / As cognizance of my blood-drinking hate, / Will I for ever and my faction wear, / Until it wither with me to my grave, / Or flourish to the height of my degree.
And by my soul, I and my party will wear this pale and angry rose forever as the badge of my bloodthirsty hatred, until it withers with me into my grave or flourishes to the height of my rank.
Go forward, and be chok'd with thy ambition! / And so farewell until I meet thee next.
