Go on, and choke on your ambition! And so goodbye until I meet you next.
Have with thee, Pole. Farewell, ambitious Richard.
I'm with you, Pole. Goodbye, ambitious Richard.
How I am braved and must perforce endure it!
How I am defied, and I must put up with it!

This blot that they object against your house / Shall be wiped out in the next parliament / Call'd for the truce of Winchester and Gloucester; / And if thou be not then created York, / I will not live to be accounted Warwick. / Meantime, in signal of my love to thee, / Against proud Somerset and William Pole, / Will I upon thy party wear this rose: / And here I prophesy: this brawl to-day, / Grown to this faction in the Temple-garden, / Shall send between the red rose and the white / A thousand souls to death and deadly night.

This stain they accuse your family of will be wiped out at the next parliament, called to make a truce between Winchester and Gloucester; and if you are not made Duke of York then, I won't live to be called Warwick. Meanwhile, as a sign of my love for you against proud Somerset and William Pole, I'll wear this rose on your side. And here I make a prophecy: this quarrel today, grown into this faction in the Temple garden, will send a thousand souls to death and endless night between the red rose and the white.
Good Master Vernon, I am bound to you, / That you on my behalf would pluck a flower.
Good Master Vernon, I'm grateful to you for picking a flower on my side.
In your behalf still will I wear the same.
I'll always wear it on your side.
Thanks, gentle sir. / Come, let us four to dinner: I dare say / This quarrel will drink blood another day.
Thank you, kind sir. Come, let's all four go to dinner. I dare say this quarrel will drink blood another day.

Kind keepers of my weak decaying age, / Let dying Mortimer here rest himself. / Even like a man new haled from the rack, / So fare my limbs with long imprisonment; / And these gray locks, the pursuivants of death, / Nestor-like aged in an age of care, / Argue the end of Edmund Mortimer. / These eyes, like lamps whose wasting oil is spent, / Wax dim, as drawing to their exigent; / Weak shoulders, overborne with burdening grief, / And pithless arms, like to a wither'd vine / That droops his sapless branches to the ground: / Yet are these feet, whose strengthless stay is numb, / Unable to support this lump of clay, / Swift-winged with desire to get a grave, / As witting I no other comfort have. / But tell me, keeper, will my nephew come?

Kind keepers of my weak, failing old age, let dying Mortimer rest here. My limbs feel like a man's just pulled off the rack, after my long imprisonment; and these grey hairs, the messengers of death, aged like Nestor's in an age of trouble, show that Edmund Mortimer's end is near. These eyes, like lamps whose oil is used up, grow dim as they come to their end. My weak shoulders are bowed with heavy grief, and my feeble arms are like a withered vine drooping its dried-up branches to the ground. Yet these feet, numb and too weak to hold up this lump of clay, are swift with desire for a grave, knowing I have no other comfort. But tell me, keeper, will my nephew come?
Richard Plantagenet, my lord, will come: / We sent unto the Temple, unto his chamber; / And answer was return'd that he will come.
Richard Plantagenet will come, my lord. We sent to his rooms at the Temple, and the answer came back that he will come.

Enough: my soul shall then be satisfied. / Poor gentleman! his wrong doth equal mine. / Since Henry Monmouth first began to reign, / Before whose glory I was great in arms, / This loathsome sequestration have I had; / And even since then hath Richard been obscured, / Deprived of honour and inheritance. / But now the arbitrator of despairs, / Just Death, kind umpire of men's miseries, / With sweet enlargement doth dismiss me hence: / I would his troubles likewise were expired, / That so he might recover what was lost.

Enough: then my soul will be satisfied. Poor gentleman! His wrongs equal mine. Ever since Henry of Monmouth began to reign (before his glory I was a great soldier), I have been kept in this hateful confinement, and ever since then Richard has been kept down, robbed of honour and inheritance. But now Death, who settles all despair, the just and kind judge of men's miseries, releases me from here with sweet freedom. I wish his troubles were over too, so that he could recover what was lost.
My lord, your loving nephew now is come.
My lord, your loving nephew has come.
Richard Plantagenet, my friend, is he come?
Richard Plantagenet, my friend, has he come?
Aye, noble uncle, thus ignobly used, / Your nephew, late despised Richard, comes.
Yes, noble uncle: your nephew, so shamefully treated, the lately despised Richard, has come.

Direct mine arms I may embrace his neck, / And in his bosom spend my latter gasp: / O, tell me when my lips do touch his cheeks, / That I may kindly give one fainting kiss. / And now declare, sweet stem from York's great stock, / Why didst thou say of late thou wert despised?

Guide my arms so that I can embrace his neck and breathe my last on his chest. Oh, tell me when my lips touch his cheeks, so I can lovingly give one faint kiss. And now tell me, sweet branch of York's great family tree, why did you say just now that you were despised?

First, lean thine aged back against mine arm; / And, in that case, I'll tell thee my disease. / This day, in argument upon a case, / Some words there grew 'twixt Somerset and me; / Among which terms he used his lavish tongue / And did upbraid me with my father's death: / Which obloquy set bars before my tongue, / Else with the like I had requited him. / Therefore, good uncle, for my father's sake, / In honor of a true Plantagenet / And for alliance sake, declare the cause / My father, Earl of Cambridge, lost his head.

First, lean your old back against my arm, and like that I'll tell you what is troubling me. Today, while arguing a case, some words arose between Somerset and me, and among them he let his tongue run wild and taunted me with my father's death. That insult silenced me, or I would have paid him back in kind. So, good uncle, for my father's sake, in honour of a true Plantagenet and for the sake of our family ties, tell me why my father, the Earl of Cambridge, lost his head.
That cause, fair nephew, that imprison'd me / And hath detain'd me all my flowering youth / Within a loathsome dungeon, there to pine, / Was cursed instrument of his decease.
Fair nephew, the same cause that imprisoned me and kept me all through my youth in a hateful dungeon to waste away was the cursed instrument of his death.
Discover more at large what cause that was, / For I am ignorant and cannot guess.
Explain more fully what that cause was, for I don't know and can't guess.

I will, if that my fading breath permit, / And death approach not ere my tale be done. / Henry the Fourth, grandfather to this king, / Deposed his nephew Richard, Edward's son, / The first-begotten and the lawful heir / Of Edward king, the third of that descent; / During whose reign the Percies of the north, / Finding his usurpation most unjust, / Endeavour'd my advancement to the throne. / The reason moved these warlike lords to this / Was, for that—young King Richard thus removed, / Leaving no heir begotten of his body— / I was the next by birth and parentage; / For by my mother I derived am / From Lionel Duke of Clarence, third son / To King Edward the Third; whereas he / From John of Gaunt doth bring his pedigree, / Being but fourth of that heroic line. / But mark: as in this haughty great attempt / They labored to plant the rightful heir, / I lost my liberty and they their lives. / Long after this, when Henry the Fifth, / Succeeding his father Bolingbroke, did reign, / Thy father, Earl of Cambridge, then derived / From famous Edmund Langley, Duke of York, / Marrying my sister that thy mother was, / Again in pity of my hard distress. / Levied an army, weening to redeem / And have install'd me in the diadem: / But, as the rest, so fell that noble earl / And was beheaded. Thus the Mortimers, / In whom the title rested, were suppress'd.

I will, if my fading breath allows and death does not come before my story is told. Henry the Fourth, grandfather of this king, deposed his cousin Richard, son of Edward the Black Prince, the eldest son and lawful heir of King Edward, the third of that name. During his reign the Percys of the north, finding his seizure of the crown most unjust, tried to put me on the throne. What moved these warlike lords to this was that, with young King Richard removed and leaving no children of his own, I was next in line by birth and descent. Through my mother I am descended from Lionel Duke of Clarence, the third son of King Edward the Third, whereas Henry traces his descent from John of Gaunt, only the fourth son of that heroic line. But note this: in that bold, great attempt to put the rightful heir on the throne, I lost my freedom and they lost their lives. Long after this, when Henry the Fifth reigned after his father Bolingbroke, your father, the Earl of Cambridge, descended from the famous Edmund Langley, Duke of York, who had married my sister, your mother, again took pity on my hard suffering and raised an army, hoping to free me and put me on the throne. But like the rest, that noble earl fell and was beheaded. So the Mortimers, in whom the right to the crown rested, were crushed.
Of which, my lord, your honor is the last.
And your lordship is the last of them.
True; and thou seest that I no issue have, / And that my fainting words do warrant death: / Thou art my heir; the rest I wish thee gather: / But yet be wary in thy studious care.
True; and you see I have no children, and my failing words are a sign of death. You are my heir; I leave the rest for you to work out. But be careful in your eager efforts.
Thy grave admonishments prevail with me: / But yet, methinks, my father's execution / Was nothing less than bloody tyranny.
Your serious warnings carry weight with me. But still, I think my father's execution was nothing less than bloody tyranny.

With silence, nephew, be thou politic: / Strong-fixed is the house of Lancaster, / And like a mountain not to be removed. / But now thy uncle is removing hence; / As princes do their courts, when they are cloy'd / With long continuance in a settled place.

Nephew, be shrewd and keep silent. The house of Lancaster is firmly fixed, like a mountain that can't be moved. But now your uncle is moving on, as princes move their courts when they are tired of staying too long in one place.
O, uncle, would some part of my young years / Might but redeem the passage of your age!
Oh, uncle, if only some of my young years could buy back your lost years!

Thou dost then wrong me, as that slaughterer doth / Which giveth many wounds when one will kill. / Mourn not, except thou sorrow for my good; / Only give order for my funeral: / And so farewell, and fair be all thy hopes, / And prosperous be thy life in peace and war!

Then you would wrong me, like a butcher who gives many wounds when one would kill. Don't mourn, unless you grieve for my good fortune. Just give orders for my funeral. And so goodbye; may all your hopes be fulfilled, and may your life prosper in peace and war!

And peace, no war, befall thy parting soul! / In prison hast thou spent a pilgrimage, / And like a hermit overpass'd thy days. / Well, I will lock his counsel in my breast; / And what I do imagine let that rest. / Keepers, convey him hence; and I myself / Will see his burial better than his life.

And may peace, not war, come to your departing soul! You have spent your life's journey in prison and passed your days like a hermit. Well, I'll lock his advice in my heart, and let what I'm thinking stay there. Keepers, carry him away; I myself will give him a better burial than he had a life.

Here dies the dusky torch of Mortimer, / Choked with ambition of the meaner sort: / And for those wrongs, those bitter injuries, / Which Somerset hath offer'd to my house, / I doubt not but with honour to redress; / And therefore haste I to the parliament, / Either to be restored to my blood, / Or make my ill the advantage of my good.

Here the dim torch of Mortimer goes out, smothered by the ambition of lesser men. And for those wrongs, those bitter injuries Somerset has done to my family, I have no doubt I'll put them right with honour. So I'm hurrying to parliament, either to be restored to my family rights or to turn my misfortune to my advantage.

Comest thou with deep premeditated lines, / With written pamphlets studiously devised, / Humphrey of Gloucester? If thou canst accuse, / Or aught intend'st to lay unto my charge. / Do it without invention, suddenly; / As I with sudden and extemporal speech / Purpose to answer what thou canst object.

Have you come with carefully planned lines, with written papers studiously put together, Humphrey of Gloucester? If you can accuse me, or mean to charge me with anything, do it on the spot, without making things up, just as I intend to answer whatever you object with an on-the-spot, unprepared speech.

Presumptuous priest! this place commands my patience, / Or thou shouldst find thou hast dishonor'd me. / Think not, although in writing I preferr'd / The manner of thy vile outrageous crimes, / That therefore I have forged, or am not able / Verbatim to rehearse the method of my pen: / No, prelate; such is thy audacious wickedness, / Thy lewd, pestiferous and dissentious pranks, / As very infants prattle of thy pride. / Thou art a most pernicious usurer, / Froward by nature, enemy to peace; / Lascivious, wanton, more than well beseems / A man of thy profession and degree; / And for thy treachery, what's more manifest / In that thou laid'st a trap to take my life, / As well at London-bridge as at the Tower. / Beside, I fear me, if thy thoughts are sifted / The king, thy sovereign, is not quite exempt / From envious malice of thy swelling heart.

Arrogant priest! This place demands my patience, or you'd find out what it means to dishonour me. Don't think that because I set out your vile, outrageous crimes in writing, I invented them or can't repeat word for word what I wrote. No, churchman: your shameless wickedness, your vile, poisonous, quarrelsome tricks are such that even babies chatter about your pride. You are a most harmful moneylender, stubborn by nature, an enemy of peace, lustful and loose-living more than is fitting for a man of your calling and rank. As for your treachery, what's more obvious than the fact that you set a trap to kill me, both at London Bridge and at the Tower? Besides, I fear that if your thoughts were examined closely, the King, your sovereign, would not be entirely safe from the envious hatred of your swollen heart.

Gloucester, I do defy thee. Lords, vouchsafe / To give me hearing what I shall reply. / If I were covetous, ambitious, or perverse, / As he will have me, how am I so poor? / Or how haps it I seek not to advance / Or raise myself, but keep my wonted calling? / And for dissension, who preferreth peace / More than I do?—except I be provoked. / No, my good lords, it is not that offends; / It is not that that hath incensed the duke: / It is, because no one should sway but he; / No one but he should be about the king; / And that engenders thunder in his breast, / And makes him roar these accusations forth. / But he shall know I am as good—

Gloucester, I defy you. Lords, be good enough to hear my reply. If I were greedy, ambitious or wicked, as he claims, how is it that I'm so poor? And how is it that I don't try to promote or raise myself, but stay in my usual calling? As for quarrelling, who prefers peace more than I do, unless I'm provoked? No, my good lords, that isn't what offends him; that isn't what has angered the Duke. It's that nobody should rule but him, nobody but him should be close to the King. That's what breeds thunder in his chest and makes him roar out these accusations. But he'll learn I am as good—
As good! / Thou bastard of my grandfather!
As good! You bastard son of my grandfather!
Aye, lordly sir; for what are you, I pray, / But one imperious in another's throne?
Yes, my lordly sir; for what are you, I'd like to know, but a man ruling arrogantly from another's throne?
Am I not protector, saucy priest?
Am I not Protector, you cheeky priest?
And am not I a prelate of the church?
And am I not a bishop of the Church?
Yes, as an outlaw in a castle keeps / And useth it to patronage his theft.
Yes, the way an outlaw holds a castle and uses it to protect his stolen goods.
Thou art reverent / Touching thy spiritual function, not thy life.
You are respected for your religious office, not for your life.
My lord, it were your duty to forbear.
My lord, it would be your duty to hold back.
Ay, see the bishop be not overborne.
Yes, make sure the bishop isn't overpowered.
Methinks my lord should be religious, / And know the office that belongs to such.
I think my lord should be religious and know the duties that go with such an office.
Methinks his lordship should be humbler; / It fitteth not a prelate so to plead.
I think his lordship should be humbler; it doesn't suit a bishop to argue like this.
Yes, when his holy state is touch'd so near.
It does, when his holy office is attacked so directly.
State holy or unhallow'd, what of that? / Is not his grace protector to the king?
Holy office or unholy, what does that matter? Isn't his Grace the King's Protector?
[Aside] Plantagenet, I see, must hold his tongue, / Lest it be said, 'Speak, sirrah, when you should: / Must your bold verdict enter talk with lords?' / Else would I have a fling at Winchester.
(Aside) I see Plantagenet must hold his tongue, or else they'll say, "Speak when you're spoken to, fellow. Must your bold opinion butt into lords' talk?" Otherwise I'd have a go at Winchester.

Uncles of Gloucester and of Winchester, / The special watchmen of our English weal, / I would prevail, if prayers might prevail, / To join your hearts in love and amity. / O, what a scandal is it to our crown, / That two such noble peers as ye should jar! / Believe me, lords, my tender years can tell / Civil dissension is a viperous worm / That gnaws the bowels of the commonwealth.

Uncles of Gloucester and Winchester, special guardians of England's welfare, I would persuade you, if prayers could do it, to join your hearts in love and friendship. Oh, what a scandal it is to our crown that two such noble lords should quarrel! Believe me, lords, even at my young age I can tell that civil strife is a poisonous worm that gnaws at the guts of the state.
An uproar, I dare warrant, / Begun through malice of the bishop's men.
A riot, I'll bet, started out of spite by the bishop's men.

O, my good lords, and virtuous Henry, / Pity the city of London, pity us! / The bishop and the Duke of Gloucester's men, / Forbidden late to carry any weapon, / Have fill'd their pockets full of pebble stones, / And banding themselves in contrary parts / Do pelt so fast at one another's pate / That many have their giddy brains knock'd out: / Our windows are broke down in every street, / And we for fear compell'd to shut our shops.

Oh, my good lords, and virtuous Henry, have pity on the city of London, pity us! The bishop's and the Duke of Gloucester's men, recently forbidden to carry any weapons, have filled their pockets with pebbles and, ganging up on opposite sides, pelt each other's heads so hard that many have had their dizzy brains knocked out. Windows are smashed in every street, and we're forced by fear to shut our shops.
We charge you, on allegiance to ourself, / To hold your slaughtering hands and keep the peace. / Pray, uncle Gloucester, mitigate this strife.
We order you, by your loyalty to us, to stop your murderous fighting and keep the peace. Please, uncle Gloucester, calm this quarrel.
Nay, if we be forbidden stones, / we'll fall to it with our teeth.
No, if we're forbidden stones, we'll go at it with our teeth.
Do what ye dare, we are as resolute.
Do what you dare; we're just as determined.
You of my household, leave this peevish broil / And set this unaccustom'd fight aside.
You of my household, stop this silly brawl and put aside this disorderly fighting.

My lord, we know your grace to be a man / Just and upright; and, for your royal birth, / Inferior to none but to his Majesty: / And ere that we will suffer such a prince, / So kind a father of the commonweal, / To be disgraced by an inkhorn mate, / We and our wives and children all will fight, / And have our bodies slaughter'd by thy foes.

My lord, we know your Grace is a just and upright man, and by royal birth second to none but his Majesty. Rather than let such a prince, so kind a father to the country, be disgraced by a pen-pushing scribbler, we and our wives and children will all fight and have our bodies slaughtered by your enemies.
Aye, and the very parings of our nails / Shall pitch a field when we are dead.
Yes, and even the clippings of our nails will set up a battle when we're dead.
Stay, stay, I say! / And if you love me, as you say you do, / Let me persuade you to forbear awhile.
Stop, stop, I say! And if you love me, as you say you do, let me persuade you to hold back a while.

O, how this discord doth afflict my soul! / Can you, my Lord of Winchester, behold / My sighs and tears and will not once relent? / Who should be pitiful, if you be not? / Or who should study to prefer a peace, / If holy churchmen take delight in broils?

Oh, how this quarrelling hurts my soul! My Lord of Winchester, can you watch my sighs and tears and not give way at all? Who should show pity, if not you? Or who should work for peace, if holy churchmen enjoy brawls?

Yield, my lord protector; yield, Winchester; / Except you mean with obstinate repulse / To slay your sovereign and destroy the realm. / You see what mischief and what murder too / Hath been enacted through your enmity; / Then be at peace, except ye thirst for blood.

Give way, Lord Protector; give way, Winchester; unless you mean to kill your king and destroy the kingdom by stubborn refusal. You see what harm, and murder too, your hostility has caused. So make peace, unless you are thirsty for blood.
He shall submit, or I will never yield.
He must submit first, or I'll never give way.
Compassion on the king commands me stoop; / Or I would see his heart out, ere the priest / Should ever get that privilege of me.
Pity for the King makes me give in; otherwise I'd see his heart cut out before the priest ever got that advantage over me.
Behold, my Lord of Winchester, the duke / Hath banish'd moody discontented fury, / As by his smoothed brows it doth appear: / Why look you still so stem and tragical?
Look, my Lord of Winchester, the Duke has driven out his sullen, discontented anger, as his smoothed brow shows. Why do you still look so stern and grim?
Here, Winchester, I offer thee my hand.
Here, Winchester, I offer you my hand.
Fie, uncle Beaufort! I have heard you preach / That malice was a great and grievous sin; / And will not you maintain the thing you teach, / But prove a chief offender in the same?
Shame, uncle Beaufort! I've heard you preach that malice was a great and terrible sin. Won't you practise what you teach, instead of proving a chief offender in it?
Sweet king! the bishop hath a kindly gird. / For shame, my lord of Winchester, relent! / What, shall a child instruct you what to do?
Sweet King! He has given the bishop a gentle dig. For shame, my Lord of Winchester, give way! What, must a child teach you what to do?
Well, Duke of Gloucester, I will yield to thee; / Love for thy love and hand for hand I give.
Well, Duke of Gloucester, I'll give way to you. I give love for your love and my hand for yours.

[Aside] Aye, but, I fear me, with a hollow heart.— / See here, my friends and loving countrymen; / This token serveth for a flag of truce / Betwixt ourselves and all our followers: / So help me God, as I dissemble not!

(Aside) Yes, but I'm afraid with a hollow heart. (Aloud) Look here, my friends and loving countrymen: this handshake serves as a flag of truce between ourselves and all our followers. So help me God, I'm not pretending!
[Aside] So help me God, as I intend it not!
(Aside) So help me God, I don't mean it at all!
O loving uncle, kind Duke of Gloucester, / How joyful am I made by this contract! / Away, my masters! trouble us no more; / But join in friendship, as your lords have done.
Oh loving uncle, kind Duke of Gloucester, how happy this agreement makes me! Away, men! Trouble us no more, but be friends, as your lords have become.
Agreed. I'll go to the surgeon's.
And I will see what physic the tavern affords.
And I'll see what medicine the tavern has to offer.
Accept this scroll, most gracious sovereign; / Which in the right of Richard Plantagenet. / We do exhibit to your majesty.
Accept this document, most gracious King, which we present to your Majesty on behalf of Richard Plantagenet's rights.

Well urged, my Lord of Warwick: for, sweet prince, / An if your Grace mark every circumstance, / You have great reason to do Richard right: / Especially for those occasions / At Eltham place I told your majesty.

Well argued, my Lord of Warwick. For, sweet Prince, if your Grace considers every circumstance, you have good reason to do Richard justice, especially for those reasons I told your Majesty at Eltham Palace.
And those occasions, uncle, were of force; / Therefore, my loving lords, our pleasure is / That Richard be restored to his blood.
And those reasons were strong, uncle. So, my loving lords, it is our wish that Richard be restored to his family rights.
Let Richard be restored to his blood; / So shall his father's wrongs be recompensed.
Let Richard be restored to his family rights; so his father's wrongs will be made up for.
As will the rest, so willeth Winchester.
As the rest wish, so does Winchester.
If Richard will be true, not that alone / But all the whole inheritance I give / That doth belong unto the house of York, / From whence you spring by lineal descent.
If Richard will be loyal, I give him not only that but the whole inheritance that belongs to the house of York, from which you are directly descended.
Thy humble servant vows obedience / And humble service till the point of death.
Your humble servant swears obedience and humble service to the point of death.

Stoop then and set your knee against my foot; / And, in reguerdon of that duty done, / I girt thee with the valiant sword of York: / Rise, Richard, like a true Plantagenet, / And rise created princely Duke of York.

Kneel then and set your knee against my foot; and as a reward for that act of loyalty, I fasten on you the brave sword of York. Rise, Richard, like a true Plantagenet, and rise made the princely Duke of York.
And so thrive Richard as thy foes may fall! / And as my duty springs, so perish they / That grudge one thought against your majesty!
May Richard thrive as surely as your enemies fall! And as my loyalty grows, so may anyone perish who holds a single grudging thought against your Majesty!
Welcome, high prince, the mighty Duke of York!
Welcome, high prince, the mighty Duke of York!
[Aside] Perish, base prince, ignoble Duke of York!
(Aside) Perish, low prince, dishonourable Duke of York!

Now will it best avail your majesty / To cross the seas and to be crown'd in France: / The presence of a king engenders love / Amongst his subjects and his loyal friends, / As it disanimates his enemies.
Now it would serve your Majesty best to cross the sea and be crowned in France. A king's presence breeds love among his subjects and loyal friends, just as it disheartens his enemies.
When Gloucester says the word, King Henry goes; / For friendly counsel cuts off many foes.
When Gloucester says the word, King Henry goes; for friendly advice cuts off many enemies.
Your ships already are in readiness.

Aye, we may march in England or in France, / Not seeing what is likely to ensue. / This late dissension grown betwixt the peers / Burns under feigned ashes of forged love, / And will at last break out into a flame; / As fest'red members rot but by degree, / Till bones and flesh and sinews fall away, / So will this base and envious discord breed. / And now I fear that fatal prophecy / Which in the time of Henry named the fifth / Was in the mouth of every sucking babe; / That Henry born at Monmouth should win all / And Henry born at Windsor lose all: / Which is so plain, that Exeter doth wish / His days may finish ere that hapless time.

Yes, we may march in England or in France without seeing what is likely to follow. This recent quarrel between the lords is burning under the false ashes of pretended love and will finally burst into flame. Just as infected limbs rot slowly until bones, flesh and sinews fall away, so this low, envious quarrel will spread. And now I fear that deadly prophecy which in the time of Henry the Fifth was on the lips of every baby: that Henry born at Monmouth would win everything, and Henry born at Windsor would lose everything. It's so obviously coming true that Exeter wishes his life may end before that unlucky time.

These are the city gates, the gates of Rouen, / Through which our policy must make a breach: / Take heed, be wary how you place your words; / Talk like the vulgar sort of market men / That come to gather money for their corn. / If we have entrance, as I hope we shall, / And that we find the slothful watch but weak, / I'll by a sign give notice to our friends, / That Charles the Dauphin may encounter them.

These are the city gates, the gates of Rouen, through which our cunning must break in. Be careful how you choose your words. Talk like ordinary market traders who come to make money from their grain. If we get in, as I hope we will, and find the lazy guard weak, I'll give a signal to our friends so that Charles the Dauphin can attack them.
Our sacks shall be a mean to sack the city, / And we be lords and rulers over Rouen; / Therefore we'll knock. [Knocks]
Our sacks will be the means to sack the city, and we'll be lords and rulers of Rouen. So we'll knock. (Knocks)
Paysans, pauvres gens de France; / Poor market folks that come to sell their corn.
Peasants, poor people of France; poor market folk who've come to sell their grain.
Enter, go in; the market bell is rung.
Come in, go in; the market bell has rung.
Now, Rouen, I'll shake thy bulwarks to the ground.
Now, Rouen, I'll shake your walls to the ground.
Saint Denis bless this happy stratagem! / And once again we'll sleep secure in Rouen.
Saint Denis bless this lucky trick! And once again we'll sleep safely in Rouen.
Here enter'd Pucelle and her practisants; / Now she is there, how will she specify / Here is the best and safest passage in?
Pucelle and her fellow plotters went in here. Now that she's inside, how will she show us which is the best and safest way in?
By thrusting out a torch from yonder tower; / Which, once discern'd, shows that her meaning is, / No way to that, for weakness, which she enter'd.
By pushing out a torch from that tower over there; once we see it, it will mean that the way she went in is the weakest.
Behold, this is the happy wedding torch / That joineth Rouen unto her countrymen, / But burning fatal to the Talbotites!
Look, this is the happy wedding torch that joins Rouen to her countrymen, but burns with death for Talbot's men!
See, noble Charles, the beacon of our friend; / The burning torch in yonder turret stands.
Look, noble Charles, our friend's beacon: the burning torch is there in that turret.
Now shine it like a comet of revenge, / A prophet to the fall of all our foes!
Now let it shine like a comet of revenge, foretelling the fall of all our enemies!
Defer no time, delays have dangerous ends; / Enter, and cry, 'The Dauphin!' presently, / And then do execution on the watch.
Don't waste time; delays end in danger. Go in at once and shout "The Dauphin!", and then kill the guards.

France, thou shalt rue this treason with thy tears, / If Talbot but survive thy treachery. / Pucelle, that witch, that damned sorceress, / Hath wrought this hellish mischief unawares, / That hardly we escaped the pride of France.

France, you'll pay for this treason with tears, if Talbot only survives your treachery. Pucelle, that witch, that damned sorceress, has done this hellish mischief by surprise, so that we barely escaped the might of France.
Good morrow, gallants! want ye corn for bread? / I think the Duke of Burgundy will fast / Before he'll buy again at such a rate: / 'Twas full of darnel: do you like the taste?
Good morning, fine gentlemen! Do you need grain for bread? I think the Duke of Burgundy will go hungry before he buys again at such a price. It was full of weeds; do you like the taste?
Scoff on, vile fiend and shameless courtezan! / I trust ere long to choke thee with thine own, / And make thee curse the harvest of that corn.
Go on mocking, vile devil and shameless whore! I hope before long to choke you with your own grain and make you curse the harvest of that corn.
Your Grace may starve perhaps before that time.
Your Grace may starve before then.
O, let no words, but deeds, revenge this treason!
Oh, let deeds, not words, avenge this treason!
What will you do, good graybeard? break a lance, / And run a tilt at death within a chair?
What will you do, good greybeard? Break a lance and charge at death in a chair?

Foul fiend of France, and hag of all despite, / Encompass'd with thy lustful paramours! / Becomes it thee to taunt his valiant age, / And twit with cowardice a man half dead? / Damsel, I'll have a bout with you again, / Or else let Talbot perish with this shame.

Foul devil of France, spiteful hag, surrounded by your lustful lovers! Is it right for you to mock his brave old age and taunt a half-dead man with cowardice? Girl, I'll have another fight with you, or else let Talbot die with this shame.
Are ye so hot? yet, Pucelle, hold thy peace; / If Talbot do but thunder, rain will follow.
Are you so heated? Still, Pucelle, keep quiet; if Talbot thunders, rain will follow.
God speed the parliament! who shall be the speaker?
God bless the parliament! Who will be the Speaker?
Dare ye come forth and meet us in the field?
Do you dare come out and meet us on the battlefield?
Belike your lordship takes us then for fools, / To try if that our own be ours or no.
Your lordship must take us for fools, to risk finding out whether what's ours is ours or not.
I speak not to that railing Hecate, / But unto thee, Alencon, and the rest; / Will ye, like soldiers, come and fight it out?
I'm not talking to that ranting witch, but to you, Alencon, and the rest. Will you come out and fight it out like soldiers?
Signior, hang! base muleters of France! / Like peasant foot-boys do they keep the walls, / And dare not take up arms like gentlemen.
Signor, go hang! Low French mule-drivers! They keep behind the walls like peasant servants and don't dare take up arms like gentlemen.
Away, captains! let 's get us from the walls; / For Talbot means no goodness by his looks. / God be wi' you, my lord! we came but to tell you / That we are here.
Away, captains! Let's get off the walls, for Talbot's looks mean us no good. God be with you, my lord! We only came to tell you we are here.

And there will we be too, ere it be long, / Or else reproach be Talbot's greatest fame! / Vow, Burgundy, by honor of thy house, / Prick'd on by public wrongs sustain'd in France, / Either to get the town again or die: / And I, as sure as English Henry lives, / And as his father here was conqueror, / As sure as in this late-betrayed town / Great Coeur-de-lion's heart was buried, / So sure I swear to get the town or die.

And we'll be there too before long, or else let disgrace be Talbot's greatest fame! Burgundy, swear by the honour of your family, spurred on by the public wrongs you've suffered in France, either to get the town back or die. And I swear, as surely as English Henry lives, as surely as his father was the conqueror here, and as surely as great Lionheart's heart was buried in this recently betrayed town, that I'll take the town or die.
My vows are equal partners with thy vows.
My vows are equal partners with yours.
But, ere we go, regard this dying prince, / The valiant Duke of Bedford. Come, my lord, / We will bestow you in some better place, / Fitter for sickness and for crazy age.
But before we go, look after this dying prince, the brave Duke of Bedford. Come, my lord, we'll move you to some better place, more suitable for sickness and frail old age.
Lord Talbot, do not so dishonor me: / Here will I sit before the walls of Rouen, / And will be partner of your weal or woe.
Lord Talbot, don't dishonour me like that. I'll sit here before the walls of Rouen and share your good or bad fortune.
Courageous Bedford, let us now persuade you.
Brave Bedford, let us persuade you now.

Not to be gone from hence; for once I read / That stout Pendragon in his litter sick / Came to the field and vanquished his foes. / Methinks I should revive the soldiers' hearts, / Because I ever found them as myself.

Not to leave here; for I once read that brave Pendragon, sick in his litter, came to the battlefield and defeated his enemies. I think I should put fresh heart into the soldiers, for I always found them like myself.
Undaunted spirit in a dying breast! / Then be it so: heavens keep old Bedford safe! / And now no more ado, brave Burgundy, / But gather we our forces out of hand / And set upon our boasting enemy.
A fearless spirit in a dying body! Then so be it. Heaven keep old Bedford safe! And now no more fuss, brave Burgundy; let's gather our forces at once and attack our boasting enemy.
Whither away, Sir John Fastolfe, in such haste?
Where are you going in such a hurry, Sir John Fastolfe?
Whither away! to save myself by flight: / We are like to have the overthrow again.
Where am I going? To save myself by running away. We're likely to be beaten again.
What! Will you fly, and leave Lord Talbot?
What! Will you run away and leave Lord Talbot?
Aye, / All the Talbots in the world, to save my life.
Yes, all the Talbots in the world, to save my life.
Cowardly knight! ill fortune follow thee!
Cowardly knight! May bad luck follow you!

Now, quiet soul, depart when heaven please, / For I have seen our enemies' overthrow. / What is the trust or strength of foolish man? / They that of late were daring with their scoffs / Are glad and fain by flight to save themselves.

Now, peaceful soul, leave when heaven pleases, for I have seen our enemies defeated. What can be trusted in foolish man, or his strength? Those who were so bold with their mocking just now are glad to save themselves by running away.
Lost, and recover'd in a day again! / This is a double honor, Burgundy: / Yet heavens have glory for this victory!
Lost and won back again in a single day! This is a double honour, Burgundy. Yet the glory for this victory belongs to heaven!
Warlike and martial Talbot, Burgundy / Enshrines thee in his heart, and there erects / Thy noble deeds as valor's monuments.
Warlike, soldierly Talbot, Burgundy enshrines you in his heart and sets up your noble deeds there as monuments to courage.

Thanks, gentle duke. But where is Pucelle now? / I think her old familiar is asleep: / Now where 's the Bastard's braves, and Charles his gleeks? / What, all amort? Rouen hangs her head for grief / That such a valiant company are fled. / Now will we take some order in the town, / Placing therein some expert officers; / And then depart to Paris to the king, / For there young Henry with his nobles lie.

Thank you, gentle Duke. But where is Pucelle now? I think her old demon is asleep. Now where is the Bastard's swaggering, and Charles's mocking? What, all dead-hearted? Rouen hangs her head in grief that such brave company has run away. Now we'll put things in order in the town, placing some experienced officers in charge, and then go to the King in Paris, for young Henry is there with his nobles.
Whatever pleases Lord Talbot pleases Burgundy.

But yet, before we go, let 's not forget / The noble Duke of Bedford late deceased, / But see his exequies fulfill'd in Rouen: / A braver soldier never couched lance, / A gentler heart did never sway in court; / But kings and mightiest potentates must die, / For that's the end of human misery.

But before we go, let's not forget the noble Duke of Bedford, who has just died; let's see his funeral carried out in Rouen. No braver soldier ever levelled a lance; no gentler heart ever ruled at court. But kings and the mightiest rulers must die, for that is the end of human misery.

Dismay not, princes, at this accident, / Nor grieve that Rouen is so recovered: / Care is no cure, but rather corrosive, / For things that are not to be remedied. / Let frantic Talbot triumph for a while / And like a peacock sweep along his tail; / We'll pull his plumes and take away his train, / If Dauphin and the rest will be but ruled.

Don't be dismayed, princes, by this setback, or grieve that Rouen has been recaptured. Worry is no cure, but rather makes worse things that can't be put right. Let frantic Talbot celebrate for a while and sweep his tail along like a peacock; we'll pluck his feathers and take away his tail if the Dauphin and the rest will just be guided by me.
We have been guided by thee hitherto, / And of thy cunning had no diffidence: / One sudden foil shall never breed distrust
We have been guided by you up to now and had no doubts about your skill. One sudden defeat will never make us distrust you.
Search out thy wit for secret policies, / And we will make thee famous through the world.
Search your mind for secret plans, and we'll make you famous throughout the world.
We'll set thy statue in some holy place, / And have thee reverenced like a blessed saint. / Employ thee then, sweet virgin, for our good.
We'll put your statue in some holy place and have you worshipped like a blessed saint. So work, sweet virgin, for our good.
Then thus it must be; this doth Joan devise: / By fair persuasions mix'd with sugar'd words / We will entice the Duke of Burgundy / To leave the Talbot and to follow us.
Then this is how it must be; this is Joan's plan: with fair persuasion mixed with sweet words, we'll tempt the Duke of Burgundy to leave Talbot and follow us.
Aye, marry, sweeting, if we could do that, / France were no place for Henry's warriors; / Nor should that nation boast it so with us, / But be extirped from our provinces.
Yes indeed, sweetheart, if we could do that, France would be no place for Henry's soldiers, and that nation wouldn't lord it over us like this, but be rooted out of our provinces.
For ever should they be expulsed from France, / And not have tide of an earldom here.
They'd be thrown out of France forever and not keep so much as an earldom here.
Your honours shall perceive how I will work / To bring this matter to the wished end.
Your lordships will see how I'll work to bring this to the end we want.
Hark! by the sound of drum you may perceive / Their powers are marching unto Paris-ward.
Listen! By the sound of the drum you can tell their forces are marching towards Paris.
There goes the Talbot, with his colors spread, / And all the troops of English after him.
There goes Talbot, with his flags flying, and all the English troops behind him.
Now in the rearward comes the duke and his: / Fortune in favor makes him lag behind. / Summon a parley; we will talk with him.
Now at the back comes the Duke and his men. Luck is on our side to make him lag behind. Call for a parley; we'll talk with him.
A parley with the Duke of Burgundy!
A parley with the Duke of Burgundy!
Who craves a parley with the Burgundy?
Who asks for a parley with Burgundy?
The princely Charles of France, thy countryman.
The princely Charles of France, your countryman.
What say'st thou, Charles? for I am marching / hence.
What do you have to say, Charles? I'm marching away from here.
Speak, Pucelle, and enchant him with thy words.
Speak, Pucelle, and enchant him with your words.
Brave Burgundy, undoubted hope of France! / Stay, let thy humble handmaid speak to thee.
Brave Burgundy, certain hope of France! Wait, let your humble servant speak to you.
Speak on; but be not over-tedious.
Speak on, but don't go on too long.

Look on thy country, look on fertile France, / And see the cities and the towns defaced / By wasting ruin of the cruel foe. / As looks the mother on her lowly babe / When death doth close his tender dying eyes, / See, see the pining malady of France; / Behold the wounds, the most unnatural wounds, / Which thou thyself hast given her woful breast. / O, turn thy edged sword another way; / Strike those that hurt, and hurt not those that help. / One drop of blood drawn from thy country's bosom / Should grieve thee more than streams of foreign gore: / Return thee therefore with a flood of tears, / And wash away thy country's stained spots.

Look at your country, look at fertile France, and see the cities and towns spoiled by the destruction of the cruel enemy. As a mother looks at her little baby when death closes its tender dying eyes, see, see the wasting sickness of France. Look at the wounds, the most unnatural wounds, that you yourself have given her sorrowful breast. Oh, turn your sharp sword another way. Strike those who hurt her, and don't hurt those who help. One drop of blood drawn from your country's breast should grieve you more than rivers of foreign blood. So come back with a flood of tears and wash away your country's stains.
Either she hath bewitch'd me with her words, / Or nature makes me suddenly relent.
Either she has bewitched me with her words or natural feeling suddenly makes me soften.

Besides, all French and France exclaims on thee, / Doubting thy birth and lawful progeny. / Who join'st thou with but with a lordly nation / That will not trust thee but for profit's sake? / When Talbot hath set footing once in France, / And fashion'd thee that instrument of ill, / Who then but English Henry will be lord, / And thou be thrust out like a fugitive? / Call we to mind, and mark but this for proof, / Was not the Duke of Orleans thy foe? / And was he not in England prisoner? / But when they heard he was thine enemy, / They set him free without his ransom paid, / In spite of Burgundy and all his friends. / See, then, thou fight'st against thy countrymen / And join'st with them will be thy slaughtermen. / Come, come, return; return, thou wandering lord; / Charles and the rest will take thee in their arms.

Besides, all the French and France itself cry out against you, doubting your birth and legitimacy. Who are you joining but an arrogant nation that will only trust you for profit? When Talbot has once got a foothold in France and made you his tool for harm, who but English Henry will be lord, and you'll be thrown out like a runaway? Let's remember, and just take this as proof: wasn't the Duke of Orleans your enemy? And wasn't he a prisoner in England? But when they heard he was your enemy, they set him free without his ransom being paid, in spite of Burgundy and all his friends. See, then, you are fighting against your own countrymen and joining those who will be your butchers. Come, come back; come back, you wandering lord. Charles and the rest will take you in their arms.

I am vanquished; these haughty words of hers / Have batt'red me like roaring cannon-shot, / And made me almost yield upon my knees. / Forgive me, country, and sweet countrymen, / And, lords, accept this hearty kind embrace: / My forces and my power of men are yours: / So, farewell, Talbot; I'll no longer trust thee.

I am beaten. These proud words of hers have battered me like roaring cannon-shot and almost brought me to my knees. Forgive me, my country and sweet countrymen; and, lords, accept this warm embrace. My forces and my troops are yours. So goodbye, Talbot; I'll trust you no longer.
[Aside] Done like a Frenchman: turn and turn / again!
(Aside) Just like a Frenchman: changing sides again and again!
Welcome, brave duke; thy friendship makes us / fresh.
Welcome, brave Duke; your friendship refreshes us.
And doth beget new courage in our breasts.
And puts new courage in our hearts.
Pucelle hath bravely play'd her part in this, / And doth deserve a coronet of gold.
Pucelle has played her part bravely in this and deserves a gold coronet.
Now let us on, my lords, and join our powers, / And seek how we may prejudice the foe.
Now let's go on, my lords, join our forces and work out how we can damage the enemy.

My gracious Prince, and honourable peers, / Hearing of your arrival in this realm, / I have awhile given truce unto my wars, / To do my duty to my sovereign: / In sign whereof, this arm, that hath reclaim'd / To your obedience fifty fortresses, / Twelve cities and seven walled towns of strength, / Beside five hundred prisoners of esteem, / Lets fall his sword before your highness' feet, / And with submissive loyalty of heart / Ascribes the glory of his conquest got / First to my God and next unto your grace. [Kneels]

My gracious Prince and honourable lords, hearing you had arrived in this kingdom, I have paused my wars for a while to pay my respects to my King. As a sign of which, this arm, which has won back for you fifty fortresses, twelve cities and seven strong walled towns, besides five hundred important prisoners, lets its sword fall at your Highness's feet and, with humble, loyal heart, gives the glory of its conquests first to my God and next to your Grace. (Kneels)
Is this the Lord Talbot, uncle Gloucester, / That hath so long been resident in France?
Is this Lord Talbot, uncle Gloucester, who has lived so long in France?
Yes, if it please your majesty, my liege.
Yes, if it please your Majesty, my lord.

Welcome, brave captain and victorious lord! / When I was young, as yet I am not old. / I do remember how my father said / A stouter champion never handled sword. / Long since we were resolved of your truth, / Your faithful service and your toil in war; / Yet never have you tasted our reward, / Or been reguerdon'd with so much as thanks. / Because till now we never saw your face: / Therefore, stand up: and for these good deserts, / We here create you Earl of Shrewsbury; / And in our coronation take your place.

Welcome, brave captain and victorious lord! When I was young (though I'm not old yet), I remember my father saying a braver champion never held a sword. We have long been sure of your loyalty, your faithful service and your hard work in war; yet you have never had a reward from us, or even been repaid with thanks, because until now we never saw your face. So stand up, and for these great services we here make you Earl of Shrewsbury; and take your place at our coronation.
Now, sir, to you, that were so hot at sea, / Disgracing of these colors that I wear / In honor of my noble Lord of York:— / Dar'st thou maintain the former words thou spakest?
Now, sir, as for you, who were so hot-tempered at sea, insulting these colours I wear in honour of my noble Lord of York: do you dare stand by the words you said before?
Yes, sir; as well as you dare patronage / The envious barking of your saucy tongue / Against my lord the Duke of Somerset.
Yes, sir, just as much as you dare defend the spiteful barking of your insolent tongue against my lord, the Duke of Somerset.
Sirrah, thy lord I honor as he is.
Fellow, I honour your lord for what he is.
Why, what is he? as good a man as York.
Why, what is he? As good a man as York.
Hark ye; not so: in witness, take ye that.
Listen: not so. As proof, take that.

Villain, thou know'st the law of arms is such / That whoso draws a sword, 'tis present death, / Or else this blow should broach thy dearest blood. / But I'll unto his majesty, and crave / I may have liberty to venge this wrong; / When thou shalt see I'll meet thee to thy cost.

Villain, you know the law of arms says that anyone who draws a sword here is put to death at once, or else this blow would let out your heart's blood. But I'll go to his Majesty and ask for permission to avenge this wrong. Then you'll see I'll meet you, and it will cost you.
Well, miscreant, I'll be there as soon as you; / And, after, meet you sooner than you would.
Well, scoundrel, I'll be there as soon as you, and afterwards meet you sooner than you'd like.
Lord bishop, set the crown upon his head.
Lord Bishop, set the crown on his head.
God save King Henry, of that name the sixth!
God save King Henry, the sixth of that name!

Now, Governor of Paris, take your oath, / That you elect no other king but him; / Esteem none friends but such as are his friends, / And none your foes but such as shall pretend / Malicious practices against his state: / This shall ye do, so help you righteous God!

Now, Governor of Paris, take your oath that you will choose no other king but him, count no one your friend but his friends and no one your enemy but those who plot evil against his rule. You will do this, so help you righteous God!
My gracious sovereign, as I rode from Calais, / To haste unto your coronation, / A letter was deliver'd to my hands, / Writ to your Grace from the Duke of Burgundy.
My gracious King, as I rode from Calais, hurrying to your coronation, a letter was put into my hands, written to your Grace by the Duke of Burgundy.

Shame to the Duke of Burgundy and thee! / I vow'd, base knight, when I did meet thee next, / To tear the garter from thy craven's leg, [Plucking it off] / Which I have done, because unworthily / Thou wast installed in that high degree. / Pardon me, princely Henry, and the rest: / This dastard, at the battle of Patay, / When but in all I was six thousand strong / And that the French were almost ten to one, / Before we met or that a stroke was given, / Like to a trusty squire did run away: / In which assault we lost twelve hundred men; / Myself and divers gentlemen beside / Were there surprised and taken prisoners. / Then judge, great lords, if I have done amiss; / Or whether that such cowards ought to wear / This ornament of knighthood, yea or no.

Shame on the Duke of Burgundy and on you! I swore, low knight, that when I met you next I'd tear the garter from your coward's leg (tearing it off), and I have done it, because you were unworthily given that high rank. Forgive me, princely Henry, and the rest of you. This coward, at the battle of Patay, when I had only six thousand men and the French outnumbered us almost ten to one, ran away like a "trusty" squire before we even met or a blow was struck. In that attack we lost twelve hundred men; I and several other gentlemen were surprised and taken prisoner. So judge, great lords, whether I have done wrong, and whether such cowards should wear this badge of knighthood or not.
To say the truth, this fact was infamous / And ill beseeming any common man, / Much more a knight, a captain, and a leader.
To tell the truth, this act was shameful and would disgrace any common man, let alone a knight, a captain and a leader.

When first this order was ordain'd, my lords, / Knights of the garter were of noble birth, / Valiant and virtuous, full of haughty courage, / Such as were grown to credit by the wars; / Not fearing death, nor shrinking for distress, / But always resolute in most extremes. / He then that is not furnish'd in this sort / Doth but usurp the sacred name of knight, / Profaning this most honorable order, / And should, if I were worthy to be judge, / Be quite degraded, like a hedge-born swain / That doth presume to boast of gentle blood.

When this order was first founded, my lords, Knights of the Garter were of noble birth, brave and virtuous, full of high courage, men who had won respect in the wars, not afraid of death or shrinking from hardship, but always determined in the greatest dangers. So anyone who doesn't have these qualities only steals the sacred name of knight, defiling this most honourable order, and should, if I were fit to judge, be completely stripped of rank, like a low-born peasant who dares to boast of noble blood.
Stain to thy countrymen, thou hear'st thy doom! / Be packing, therefore, thou that wast a knight; / Henceforth we banish thee, on pain of death.
Disgrace to your countrymen, you hear your sentence! Get out, then, you who were a knight. From now on we banish you, on pain of death.
And now, my lord protector, view the letter / Sent from our uncle Duke of Burgundy.
And now, Lord Protector, read the letter sent from our uncle, the Duke of Burgundy.

What means his grace, / that he hath changed his style? / No more but, plain and bluntly, 'To the King!' / Hath he forgot he is his sovereign? / Or doth this churlish superscription / Pretend some alteration in good will? / What's here? [Reads] 'I have, upon especial cause, / Moved with compassion of my country's wreck, / Together with the pitiful complaints / Of such as your oppression feeds upon, / Forsaken your pernicious faction, / And join'd with Charles, the rightful King of France.' / O monstrous treachery! can this be so, / That in alliance, amity and oaths, / There should be found such false dissembling guile?

What does his Grace mean by changing the way he addresses me? Nothing more than, plain and blunt, "To the King!" Has he forgotten he's his king? Or does this rude address mean some change in his loyalty? What's here? (Reads) "For special reasons, moved by pity for my country's ruin and by the pitiful complaints of those your oppression preys on, I have abandoned your harmful party and joined Charles, the rightful King of France." Oh, monstrous treachery! Can it be that such false, deceitful cunning should be found in alliance, friendship and sworn oaths?
What! doth my uncle Burgundy revolt?
What! Has my uncle Burgundy rebelled?
He doth, my lord, and is become your foe.
He has, my lord, and has become your enemy.
Is that the worst this letter doth contain?
Is that the worst the letter contains?
It is the worst, and all, my lord, he writes.
That's the worst, and all he writes, my lord.
Why, then, Lord Talbot there shall talk with him, / And give him chastisement for this abuse. / How say you, my lord? are you not content?
Why, then, Lord Talbot here will talk with him and punish him for this wrong. What do you say, my lord? Are you willing?
Content, my liege! yes; but that I am prevented, / I should have begg'd I might have been employ'd.
Willing, my lord! Yes; if you hadn't got in first, I would have begged to be sent.
Then gather strength, and march unto him straight: / Let him perceive how ill we brook his treason. / And what offence it is to flout his friends.
Then gather your forces and march straight at him. Let him see how badly we take his treason and what an offence it is to mock his friends.
I go, my lord, in heart desiring still / You may behold confusion of your foes.
I'm going, my lord, with all my heart wishing that you may see your enemies destroyed.
Grant me the combat, gracious sovereign.
Allow me a duel, gracious King.
And me, my lord, grant me the combat too.
And me, my lord; allow me the duel too.
This is my servant: hear him, noble prince.
This is my servant; listen to him, noble Prince.
And this is mine: sweet Henry, favor him.
And this is mine; sweet Henry, favour him.
Be patient, lords, and give them leave to speak. / Say, gentlemen, what makes you thus exclaim? / And wherefore crave you combat? or with whom?
Be patient, lords, and let them speak. Tell me, gentlemen, why are you shouting like this? Why do you ask for a duel, and with whom?
With him, my lord; for he hath done me wrong.
With him, my lord, for he has wronged me.
And I with him; for he hath done me wrong.
And I with him, for he has wronged me.
What is that wrong whereof you both complain? / First let me know, and then I'll answer you.
What is this wrong you both complain of? Let me know first, and then I'll answer you.

Crossing the sea from England into France, / This fellow here, with envious carping tongue, / Upbraided me about the rose I wear; / Saying, the sanguine colour of the leaves / Did represent my master's blushing cheeks, / When stubbornly he did repugn the truth / About a certain question in the law / Argued betwixt the Duke of York and him; / With other vile and ignominious terms: / In confutation of which rude reproach, / And in defence of my lord's worthiness, / I crave the benefit of law of arms.

Crossing the sea from England to France, this fellow here, with his spiteful, sneering tongue, taunted me about the rose I wear, saying the blood-red colour of its petals stood for my master's blushing cheeks when he stubbornly denied the truth in a certain legal question argued between him and the Duke of York; and other vile and shameful things. To answer that rude insult and defend my lord's honour, I ask for my right under the law of arms.

And that is my petition, noble lord: / For though he seem with forged quaint conceit / To set a gloss upon his bold intent, / Yet know, my lord, I was provoked by him; / And he first took exceptions at this badge, / Pronouncing that the paleness of this flower / Bewray'd the faintness of my master's heart.

And that is my request, noble lord. For though he tries to put a fine gloss on his bold intentions with clever made-up stories, know, my lord, that he provoked me. He first found fault with this badge, saying the paleness of this flower revealed the cowardice of my master's heart.
Will not this malice, Somerset, be left?
Somerset, won't you drop this spite?
Your private grudge, my Lord of York, will out, / Though ne'er so cunningly you smother it.
Your private grudge will come out, my Lord of York, however cleverly you hide it.

Good Lord, what madness rules in brainsick men, / When for so slight and frivolous a cause / Such factious emulations shall arise! / Good cousins both, of York and Somerset, / Quiet yourselves, I pray, and be at peace.
Good Lord, what madness rules in sick-brained men, when such party rivalries spring up from so small and silly a cause! Good kinsmen both, York and Somerset, calm down, please, and be at peace.
Let this dissension first be tried by fight, / And then your highness shall command a peace.
Let this quarrel be settled by a fight first, and then your Highness can order peace.
The quarrel toucheth none but us alone; / Betwixt ourselves let us decide it then.
The quarrel concerns no one but us; so let's decide it between ourselves.
There is my pledge; accept it, Somerset.
There's my glove as a challenge; take it, Somerset.
Nay, let it rest where it began at first.
No, let it stay where it first began.
Confirm it so, mine honorable lord.
Agree to that, my honourable lord.

Confirm it so! Confounded be your strife! / And perish ye, with your audacious prate! / Presumptuous vassals, are you not ashamed / With this immodest clamorous outrage / To trouble and disturb the king and us? / And you, my lords, methinks you do not well / To bear with their perverse objections; / Much less to take occasion from their mouths / To raise a mutiny betwixt yourselves: / Let me persuade you take a better course.

Agree to that! Damn your quarrel! And may you perish with your bold chatter! Arrogant servants, aren't you ashamed to trouble and disturb the King and us with this rude, noisy outrage? And you, my lords, I don't think you do well to put up with their wrong-headed complaints, much less to take the chance from their mouths to start a mutiny among yourselves. Let me persuade you to take a better course.
It grieves his highness: good my lords, be friends.
It upsets his Highness. My good lords, be friends.

Come hither, you that would be combatants: / Henceforth I charge you, as you love our favor, / Quite to forget this quarrel and the cause. / And you, my lords, remember where we are: / In France, amongst a fickle wavering nation; / If they perceive dissension in our looks / And that within ourselves we disagree, / How will their grudging stomachs be provoked / To willful disobedience, and rebel! / Beside, what infamy will there arise / When foreign princes shall be certified / That for a toy, a thing of no regard, / King Henry's peers and chief nobility / Destroy'd themselves and lost the realm of France / O, think upon the conquest of my father, / My tender years; and let us not forgo / That for a trifle that was bought with blood! / Let me be umpire in this doubtful strife. / I see no reason, if I wear this rose,

Come here, you who want to fight. From now on, as you value our favour, I order you to forget this quarrel and its cause completely. And you, my lords, remember where we are: in France, among a fickle, unreliable nation. If they see disagreement in our faces and that we're quarrelling among ourselves, how their resentful hearts will be stirred to wilful disobedience and rebellion! Besides, what disgrace will follow when foreign princes hear that King Henry's lords and chief nobles destroyed themselves and lost the kingdom of France over a trifle, a thing of no importance! Oh, think of my father's conquests and my young age, and let's not throw away for a trifle what was bought with blood! Let me be the judge in this uncertain quarrel. I see no reason, if I wear this rose (putting on a red rose),

That any one should therefore be suspicious / I more incline to Somerset than York: / Both are my kinsmen, and I love them both: / As well they may upbraid me with my crown, / Because, forsooth, the king of Scots is crown'd. / But your discretions better can persuade / Than I am able to instruct or teach; / And, therefore, as we hither came in peace, / So let us still continue peace and love. / Cousin of York, we institute your grace / To be our Regent in these parts of France: / And, good my Lord of Somerset, unite / Your troops of horsemen with his bands of foot; / And, like true subjects, sons of your progenitors, / Go cheerfully together and digest / Your angry choler on your enemies. / Ourself, my lord protector and the rest / After some respite will return to Calais; / From thence to England; where I hope ere long / To be presented, by your victories, / With Charles, Alencon, and that traitorous rout.

why anyone should suspect that I lean more towards Somerset than York. Both are my relatives, and I love them both. They might just as well blame me for my crown because, of course, the King of Scots is crowned too. But your own good sense can persuade you better than I can instruct or teach; so, as we came here in peace, let's keep on in peace and love. Cousin of York, we appoint your Grace our Regent in these parts of France. And, my good Lord of Somerset, join your cavalry with his foot soldiers, and like true subjects and sons of your ancestors, go cheerfully together and spend your angry temper on your enemies. I, the Lord Protector and the rest will return to Calais after a short rest, and from there to England, where I hope before long that your victories will present me with Charles, Alencon and that traitorous mob.
My Lord of York, I promise you, the king / Prettily, methought, did play the orator.
My Lord of York, I promise you, I thought the King played the speaker rather nicely.
And so he did; but yet I like it not, / In that he wears the badge of Somerset.
So he did; but I don't like the fact that he wears Somerset's badge.
Tush, that was but his fancy, blame him not; / I dare presume, sweet prince, he thought no harm.
Pooh, that was just a whim; don't blame him. I dare say, sweet Prince, he meant no harm.
An if I wist he did,—but let it rest; / Other affairs must now be managed.
If I knew he did— but let it go. Other business must be dealt with now.

Well didst thou, Richard, to suppress thy voice; / For, had the passions of thy heart burst out, / I fear we should have seen decipher'd there / More rancorous spite, more furious raging broils, / Than yet can be imagined or supposed. / But howsoe'er, no simple man that sees / This jarring discord of nobility, / This shouldering of each other in the court, / This factious bandying of their favorites, / But that it doth presage some ill event. / Tis much when scepters are in children's hands; / But more when envy breeds unkind division; / There comes the ruin, there begins confusion.

You did well, Richard, to keep quiet; for if the feelings of your heart had burst out, I fear we would have seen revealed there more bitter spite and more furious, raging quarrels than can yet be imagined. But in any case, no simple man who sees this clashing discord among the nobles, this shoving at each other in court, this factional fighting among their followers, could fail to see that it foretells some evil outcome. It's bad enough when a child holds the sceptre, but worse when envy breeds unnatural division. That's where ruin comes; that's where chaos begins.
Go to the gates of Bordeaux, trumpeter: / Summon their general unto the wall.
Go to the gates of Bordeaux, trumpeter, and call their general to the wall.

English John Talbot, Captains, calls you forth, / Servant in arms to Harry King of England; / And thus he would: Open your city-gates, / Be humble to us; call my sovereign yours, / And do him homage as obedient subjects; / And I'll withdraw me and my bloody power: / But, if you frown upon this proffer'd peace, / You tempt the fury of my three attendants, / Lean famine, quartering steel, and climbing fire; / Who in a moment even with the earth / Shall lay your stately and air-braving towers, / If you forsake the offer of their love.

Captains, English John Talbot calls you out, a soldier in the service of Harry, King of England, and this is what he wants: open your city gates, submit to us, call my king your king and pay him homage as obedient subjects, and I'll withdraw myself and my bloody army. But if you frown on this offer of peace, you provoke the fury of my three servants, thin famine, cutting steel and climbing fire, who will in a moment level your grand, sky-defying towers with the earth if you reject their offer of love.

Thou ominous and fearful owl of death, / Our nation's terror and their bloody scourge! / The period of thy tyranny approacheth. / On us thou canst not enter but by death; / For, I protest, we are well fortified / And strong enough to issue out and fight: / If thou retire, the Dauphin, well appointed, / Stands with the snares of war to tangle thee: / On either hand thee there are squadrons pitch'd / To wall thee from the liberty of flight; / And no way canst thou turn thee for redress, / But death doth front thee with apparent spoil, / And pale destruction meets thee in the face. / Ten thousand French have ta'en the sacrament / To rive their dangerous artillery / Upon no Christian soul but English Talbot. / Lo, there thou stand'st, a breathing valiant man, / Of an invincible unconquer'd spirit! / This is the latest glory of thy praise / That I, thy enemy, due thee withal; / For ere the glass, that now begins to run, / Finish the process of his sandy hour, / These eyes, that see thee now well colored, / Shall see thee wither'd, bloody, pale, and dead.

You ominous, fearful owl of death, our nation's terror and its bloody scourge! The end of your tyranny is coming. You can't get in to us except through death, for I declare we're well fortified and strong enough to come out and fight. If you retreat, the Dauphin, well equipped, is waiting with the traps of war to catch you. There are troops set on both sides of you to wall you off from escape, and there's no way you can turn for help without death facing you with certain ruin and pale destruction meeting you face to face. Ten thousand French have sworn on the sacrament to fire their deadly cannon at no Christian soul but English Talbot. Look, there you stand, a living brave man of unbeatable, unconquered spirit! This is the last praise I, your enemy, will give you; for before this hourglass, which is just starting to run, finishes its sandy hour, these eyes that see you now healthy will see you withered, bloody, pale and dead.
Hark! hark! the Dauphin's drum, a warning bell, / Sings heavy music to thy timorous soul; / And mine shall ring thy dire departure out.
Listen! Listen! The Dauphin's drum, a warning bell, sings sad music to your fearful soul, and mine will ring out your dreadful death.

He fables not; I hear the enemy: / Out, some light horsemen, and peruse their wings. / O, negligent and heedless discipline! / How are we park'd and bounded in a pale, / A little herd of England's timorous deer, / Mazed with a yelping kennel of French curs! / If we be English deer, be then in blood; / Not rascal-like, to fall down with a pinch, / But rather, moody-mad and desperate stags, / Turn on the bloody hounds with heads of steel / And make the cowards stand aloof at bay: / Sell every man his life as dear as mine, / And they shall find dear deer of us, my friends. / God and Saint George, Talbot and England's right, / Prosper our colors in this dangerous fight!

He's not making it up; I hear the enemy. Out, some light horsemen, and scout their flanks. Oh, careless, thoughtless discipline! How we are penned and fenced in, a little herd of England's timid deer, bewildered by a yelping pack of French dogs! If we are English deer, then let us be in full vigour, not like weak deer that fall at a nip, but rather like angry, desperate stags; turn on the bloody hounds with heads of steel and make the cowards keep their distance. Let every man sell his life as dearly as I sell mine, and they'll find us dear deer, my friends. God and Saint George, Talbot and England's right, bless our flags in this dangerous fight!
Are not the speedy scouts return'd again, / That dogg'd the mighty army of the Dauphin?
Haven't the fast scouts come back yet, who were following the Dauphin's mighty army?

They are return'd, my lord, and give it out / That he is march'd to Bordeaux with his power, / To fight with Talbot: as he march'd along, / By your espials were discovered / Two mightier troops than that the Dauphin led, / Which join'd with him and made their march for / Bordeaux.

They have come back, my lord, and report that he has marched to Bordeaux with his army to fight Talbot. As he marched along, your spies discovered two larger forces than the one the Dauphin led, which joined up with him and set out for Bordeaux.

A plague upon that villain Somerset, / That thus delays my promised supply / Of horsemen, that were levied for this siege! / Renowned Talbot doth expect my aid, / And I am lowted by a traitor villain, / And cannot help the noble chevalier: / God comfort him in this necessity! / If he miscarry, farewell wars in France.

A plague on that villain Somerset, who is holding back the cavalry I was promised, raised for this siege! Famous Talbot is expecting my help, and I'm made a fool of by a treacherous villain and can't help the noble knight. God comfort him in this need! If he fails, goodbye to the wars in France.

Thou princely leader of our English strength, / Never so needful on the earth of France, / Spur to the rescue of the noble Talbot, / Who now is girdled with a waist of iron, / And hemm'd about with grim destruction. / To Bordeaux, warlike Duke! to Bordeaux, York! / Else, farewell, Talbot, France, and England's honor.

Princely leader of our English forces, never so needed on French soil, ride hard to the rescue of noble Talbot, who is now surrounded by a belt of iron and hemmed in by grim destruction. To Bordeaux, warlike Duke! To Bordeaux, York! Or else goodbye to Talbot, France and England's honour.

O God, that Somerset, who in proud heart / Doth stop my cornets, were in Talbot's place! / So should we save a valiant gentleman / By forfeiting a traitor and a coward. / Mad ire and wrathful fury makes me weep, / That thus we die, while remiss traitors sleep.

Oh God, if only Somerset, who in his pride holds back my cavalry, were in Talbot's place! Then we would save a brave gentleman by losing a traitor and a coward. Mad anger and furious rage make me weep that we die like this while lazy traitors sleep.
O, send some succor to the distress'd lord!
Oh, send some help to the lord in danger!
He dies; we lose; I break my warlike word; / We mourn, France smiles; we lose, they daily get; / All 'long of this vile traitor Somerset.
He dies; we lose; I break my soldier's word. We mourn, France smiles; we lose, they gain every day; all because of this vile traitor Somerset.

Then God take mercy on brave Talbot's soul; / And on his son young John, who two hours since / I met in travel toward his warlike father! / This seven years did not Talbot see his son; / And now they meet where both their lives are done.

Then God have mercy on brave Talbot's soul, and on his son young John, whom I met two hours ago travelling towards his warlike father! For seven years Talbot hasn't seen his son, and now they meet where both their lives will end.

Alas, what joy shall noble Talbot have, / To bid his young son welcome to his grave? / Away! vexation almost stops my breath, / That sunder'd friends greet in the hour of death. / Lucy, farewell: no more my fortune can, / But curse the cause I cannot aid the man. / Maine, Blois, Poictiers, and Tours, are won away, / 'Long all of Somerset and his delay.

Alas, what joy will noble Talbot have in welcoming his young son to his grave? Away! Anguish almost stops my breath, that separated loved ones meet at the hour of death. Lucy, goodbye. My fortune can do no more than curse the cause that I can't help the man. Maine, Blois, Poitiers and Tours are lost, all because of Somerset and his delay.

Thus, while the vulture of sedition / Feeds in the bosom of such great commanders, / Sleeping neglection doth betray to loss / The conquest of our scarce cold conqueror, / That ever living man of memory, / Henry the Fifth: whiles they each other cross, / Lives, honors, lands and all hurry to loss.

So while the vulture of rebellion feeds in the hearts of such great commanders, sleepy neglect loses the conquests of our hardly cold conqueror, Henry the Fifth, that man who will live forever in memory. While they block each other, lives, honours, lands and everything rush to ruin.

It is too late; I cannot send them now: / This expedition was by York and Talbot / Too rashly plotted: all our general force / Might with a sally of the very town / Be buckled with: the over-daring Talbot / Hath sullied all his gloss of former honor / By this unheedful, desperate, wild adventure: / York set him on to fight and die in shame, / That, Talbot dead, great York might bear the name.

It's too late; I can't send them now. York and Talbot planned this expedition too rashly. Our whole army could have been taken on by a single sortie from the town. Over-bold Talbot has tarnished all the shine of his former honour by this careless, desperate, wild venture. York sent him to fight and die in shame so that, with Talbot dead, great York could have the fame.
Here is Sir William Lucy, who with me / Set from our o'er-match'd forces forth for aid.
Here is Sir William Lucy, who set out with me from our outnumbered forces to get help.
How now, Sir William! whither were you sent?
What now, Sir William! Where were you sent from?
