Whither, my lord? from bought and sold Lord Talbot; / Who, ring'd about with bold adversity, / Cries out for noble York and Somerset, / To beat assailing death from his weak legions; / And whiles the honorable captain there / Drops bloody sweat from his war-wearied limbs, / And, in advantage lingering, looks for rescue, / You, his false hopes, the trust of England's honor, / Keep off aloof with worthless emulation. / Let not your private discord keep away / The levied succors that should lend him aid, / While he, renowned noble gentleman, / Yield up his life unto a world of odds. / Orleans the Bastard, Charles, Burgundy, / Alencon, Reignier, compass him about, / And Talbot perisheth by your default.

Where from, my lord? From Lord Talbot, betrayed and sold, who, ringed around with bold danger, calls for noble York and Somerset to beat back attacking death from his weak troops. And while that honourable captain drips bloody sweat from his war-weary limbs, holding out and looking for rescue, you, his false hopes, the trustees of England's honour, keep your distance in worthless rivalry. Don't let your private quarrel keep away the reinforcements raised to help him, while he, a famous, noble gentleman, gives up his life against overwhelming odds. The Bastard of Orleans, Charles, Burgundy, Alencon and Reignier surround him, and Talbot dies through your failure.
York set him on; York should have sent him aid.
York sent him into it; York should have sent him help.
And York as fast upon your grace exclaims; / Swearing that you withhold his levied host, / Collected for this expedition.
And York cries out just as hard against your Grace, swearing that you are holding back the forces he raised for this expedition.
York lies; he might have sent and had the horse: / I owe him little duty, and less love; / And take foul scorn to fawn on him by sending.
York lies. He could have sent for the cavalry and had it. I owe him little duty and less love, and I'd scorn to fawn on him by sending it unasked.
The fraud of England, not the force of France, / Hath now entrapp'd the noble-minded Talbot: / Never to England shall he bear his life; / But dies, betray'd to fortune by your strife.
English deceit, not French strength, has now trapped noble-minded Talbot. He'll never bring his life back to England, but dies, betrayed to fortune by your quarrel.
Come, go; I will dispatch the horsemen straight: / Within six hours they will be at his aid.
Come, go; I'll send the cavalry at once. They'll reach him within six hours.
Too late comes rescue; he is ta'en or slain; / For fly he could not, if he would have fled; / And fly would Talbot never, though he might.
Help comes too late. He's captured or killed; for he couldn't have run if he'd wanted to, and Talbot would never run even if he could.
If he be dead, brave Talbot, then adieu!
If he's dead, then farewell, brave Talbot!
His fame lives in the world, his shame in you.
His fame lives on in the world, his shame in you.

O young John Talbot! I did send for thee / To tutor thee in stratagems of war, / That Talbot's name might be in thee revived / When sapless age and weak unable limbs / Should bring thy father to his drooping chair. / But, O malignant and ill-boding stars! / Now thou art come unto a feast of death, / A terrible and unavoided danger: / Therefore, dear boy, mount on my swiftest horse; / And I'll direct thee how thou shalt escape / By sudden flight: come, dally not, be gone.

Oh, young John Talbot! I sent for you to teach you the tactics of war, so that Talbot's name might live again in you when dried-up old age and weak, useless limbs bring your father to his invalid chair. But oh, evil and ill-omened stars! Now you have come to a feast of death, a terrible and unavoidable danger. So, dear boy, get on my fastest horse, and I'll show you how to escape by fleeing at once. Come, don't delay; go.

Is my name Talbot? and am I your son? / And shall I fly? O, if you love my mother, / Dishonor not her honorable name, / To make a bastard and a slave of me! / The world will say, he is not Talbot's blood, / That basely fled when noble Talbot stood.

Is my name Talbot? And am I your son? And should I run away? Oh, if you love my mother, don't dishonour her good name by making me a bastard and a coward! The world will say he isn't Talbot's flesh and blood who ran away like a coward when noble Talbot stood his ground.
Fly, to revenge my death, if I be slain.
Run, to avenge my death if I am killed.
He that flies so will ne'er return again.
Whoever runs like that will never come back.
If we both stay, we both are sure to die.
If we both stay, we're both sure to die.

Then let me stay; and, father, do you fly; / Your loss is great, so your regard should be; / My worth unknown, no loss is known in me. / Upon my death the French can little boast; / In yours they will, in you all hopes are lost. / Flight cannot stain the honor you have won; / But mine it will, that no exploit have done; / You fled for vantage, every one will swear; / But, if I bow, they'll say it was for fear. / There is no hope that ever I will stay, / If the first hour I shrink and run away. / Here on my knee I beg mortality, / Rather than life preserved with infamy.

Then let me stay, and you run, father. Your loss is great, so you should look after yourself; my worth is unknown, so no loss will be felt in me. The French can't boast much about my death; they will about yours, for all hopes rest in you. Running away can't stain the honour you have won, but it will stain mine, since I've done no great deed. Everyone will swear you ran for good tactical reasons; but if I give way, they'll say it was from fear. There's no hope that I'll ever stand firm if I shrink and run away in my first hour. Here on my knee I beg for death rather than life saved with disgrace.
Shall all thy mother's hopes lie in one tomb?
Are all your mother's hopes to lie in one tomb?
Aye, rather than I'll shame my mother's womb.
Yes, rather than shame my mother's womb.
Upon my blessing, I command thee go.
On my blessing, I order you to go.
To fight I will, but not to fly the foe.
I'll go to fight, but not to run from the enemy.
Part of thy father may be saved in thee.
Part of your father may be saved in you.
No part of him but will be shame in me.
No part of him that won't be shame in me.
Thou never hadst renown, nor canst not lose it.
You never had fame, so you can't lose it.
Yes, your renowned name: shall flight abuse it?
Yes, your famous name. Shall running away disgrace it?
Thy father's charge shall clear thee from that stain.
Your father's order will clear you of that stain.
You cannot witness for me, being slain. / If death be so apparent, then both fly.
You can't speak up for me once you're dead. If death is so certain, then let's both run.
And leave my followers here to fight and die; / My age was never tainted with such shame.
And leave my followers here to fight and die? My old age was never stained with such shame.

And shall my youth be guilty of such blame? / No more can I be sever'd from your side, / Than can yourself yourself in twain divide: / Stay, go, do what you will, the like do I; / For live I will not, if my father die.

And shall my youth be guilty of such blame? I can no more be separated from your side than you can split yourself in two. Stay, go, do what you like, I'll do the same; for I won't live if my father dies.
Then here I take my leave of thee, fair son, / Born to eclipse thy life this afternoon. / Come, side by side together live and die; / And soul with soul from France to heaven fly.
Then here I say goodbye to you, fair son, born to have your life put out this afternoon. Come, side by side let's live and die together, and fly soul with soul from France to heaven.

Saint George and victory; fight, soldiers, fight: / The regent hath with Talbot broke his word, / And left us to the rage of France his sword. / Where is John Talbot? Pause, and take thy breath; / I gave thee life and rescued thee from death.

Saint George and victory! Fight, soldiers, fight! The Regent has broken his word to Talbot and left us to the fury of France's sword. Where is John Talbot? Stop and get your breath. I gave you life, and now I've rescued you from death.
O, twice my father, twice am I thy son! / The life thou gavest me first was lost and done, / Till with thy warlike sword, despite of fate, / To my determined time thou gavest new date.
Oh, twice my father, twice I am your son! The life you first gave me was lost and finished, until, in spite of fate, your warlike sword gave my appointed time a new date.

When from the Dauphin's crest thy sword struck fire, / It warm'd thy father's heart with proud desire / Of bold-faced victory. Then leaden age, / Quicken'd with youthful spleen and warlike rage, / Beat down Alencon, Orleans, Burgundy, / And from the pride of Gallia rescued thee. / The ireful bastard Orleans, that drew blood / From thee, my boy, and had the maidenhood / Of thy first fight, I soon encountered, / And interchanging blows I quickly shed / Some of his bastard blood; and in disgrace / Bespoke him thus; 'Contaminated base / And misbegotten blood I spill of thine, / Mean and right poor, for that pure blood of mine, / Which thou didst force from Talbot, my brave boy:' / Here, purposing the Bastard to destroy, / Came in strong rescue. Speak, thy father's care, / Art thou not weary, John? how dost thou fare? / Wilt thou yet leave the battle, boy, and fly, / Now thou art seal'd the son of chivalry? / Fly, to revenge my death when I am dead: / The help of one stands me in little stead. / O, too much folly is it, well I wot, / To hazard all our lives in one small boat! / If I to-day die not with Frenchmen's rage, / To-morrow I shall die with mickle age: / By me they nothing gain an if I stay; / 'Tis but the short'ning of my life one day: / In thee thy mother dies, our household's name, / My death's revenge, thy youth, and England's fame: / All these and more we hazard by thy stay; / All these are saved if thou wilt fly away.

When your sword struck sparks from the Dauphin's helmet, it warmed your father's heart with proud desire for bold victory. Then my heavy old age, quickened with young fire and warlike rage, beat down Alencon, Orleans and Burgundy and rescued you from the pride of France. The angry Bastard of Orleans, who drew blood from you, my boy, and had the first taste of your first fight, I soon met, and exchanging blows I quickly spilled some of his bastard blood, and insulted him like this: "I spill your tainted, low, illegitimate blood, mean and worthless, in return for my pure blood, which you forced from Talbot, my brave boy." Here, as I meant to kill the Bastard, strong help came to rescue him. Speak, you who are your father's worry: aren't you tired, John? How are you? Will you leave the battle now, boy, and run, now that you're confirmed as the son of knighthood? Run, to avenge my death when I am dead. The help of one man is little use to me. Oh, I know well it's too foolish to risk all our lives in one small boat! If I don't die today from French rage, I'll die tomorrow from great age. They gain nothing if I stay; it only shortens my life by a day. In you die your mother, our family's name, the revenge for my death, your youth and England's fame. We risk all these and more if you stay; all these are saved if you'll run away.

The sword of Orleans hath not made me smart; / These words of yours draw life-blood from my heart: / On that advantage, bought with such a shame, / To save a paltry life and slay bright fame, / Before young Talbot from old Talbot fly, / The coward horse that bears me fall and die! / And like me to the peasant boys of France, / To be shame's scorn and subject of mischance! / Surely, by all the glory you have won, / An if I fly, I am not Talbot's son; / Then talk no more of flight, it is no boot; / If son to Talbot, die at Talbot's foot.

The sword of Orleans didn't make me suffer; these words of yours draw blood from my heart. Rather than young Talbot run from old Talbot for that advantage, bought with such shame, to save a worthless life and kill bright fame, may the cowardly horse that carries me fall and die! And may I be compared to the peasant boys of France, mocked by shame and a target for bad luck! Surely, by all the glory you have won, if I run, I'm not Talbot's son. So say no more about running; it's no use. If I'm Talbot's son, I'll die at Talbot's feet.
Then follow thou thy desperate sire of Crete, / Thou Icarus; thy life to me is sweet: / If thou wilt fight, fight by thy father's side; / And, commendable proved, let 's die in pride.
Then follow your desperate father of Crete, you Icarus. Your life is sweet to me. If you will fight, fight by your father's side, and having proved our worth, let's die in pride.

Where is my other life? mine own is gone; / O, where's young Talbot? where is valiant John? / Triumphant death, smear'd with captivity, / Young Talbot's valor makes me smile at thee: / When he perceived me shrink and on my knee, / His bloody sword he brandish'd over me, / And, like a hungry lion, did commence / Rough deeds of rage and stern impatience; / But when my angry guardant stood alone, / Tendering my ruin and assail'd of none, / Dizzy-ey'd fury and great rage of heart / Suddenly made him from my side to start / Into the clustering battle of the French; / And in that sea of blood my boy did drench / His over-mounting spirit, and there died, / My Icarus, my blossom, in his pride.

Where is my other life? My own is gone. Oh, where's young Talbot? Where is brave John? Triumphant Death, stained with my captivity, young Talbot's courage makes me smile at you. When he saw me sink to my knee, he waved his bloody sword over me and, like a hungry lion, began rough deeds of rage and fierce impatience. But when my angry guardian stood alone, watching over my fall and attacked by no one, dizzy fury and great rage of heart suddenly made him leap from my side into the crowded ranks of the French. And in that sea of blood my boy drowned his soaring spirit, and there died, my Icarus, my blossom, in his pride.
O my dear lord, lo where your son is borne!
Oh, my dear lord, look, here your son is carried!

Thou antic Death, which laugh'st us here to scorn, / Anon, from thy insulting tyranny, / Coupled in bonds of perpetuity, / Two Talbots, winged through the lither sky, / In thy despite shall 'scape mortality. / O thou, whose wounds become hard-favor'd death, / Speak to thy father ere thou yield thy breath! / Brave death by speaking, whether he will or no; / Imagine him a Frenchman and thy foe. / Poor boy! he smiles, methinks, as who should say, / Had death been French, then death had died to-day. / Come, come and lay him in his father's arms: / My spirit can no longer bear these harms. / Soldiers, adieu! I have what I would have, / Now my old arms are young John Talbot's grave.

You grinning clown Death, who laughs at us here in scorn, soon, coupled in everlasting bonds, two Talbots, flying through the yielding sky, will escape from your insulting tyranny and from death, in spite of you. Oh you, whose wounds make ugly death look handsome, speak to your father before you breathe your last! Defy death by speaking, whether he likes it or not; imagine he's a Frenchman and your enemy. Poor boy! I think he smiles, as if to say that if death had been French, death would have died today. Come, come and lay him in his father's arms. My spirit can't bear these hurts any longer. Soldiers, goodbye! I have what I wanted: now my old arms are young John Talbot's grave.
Had York and Somerset brought rescue in, / We should have found a bloody day of this.
If York and Somerset had brought reinforcements, this would have been a bloody day for us.
How the young whelp of Talbot's, raging-wood, / Did flesh his puny sword in Frenchmen's blood!
How Talbot's young cub, raging mad, gave his little sword its first taste of French blood!

Once I encounter'd him, and thus I said: / 'Thou maiden youth, be vanquish'd by a maid.' / But, with a proud majestical high scorn, / He answer'd thus: 'Young Talbot was not born / To be the pillage of a giglot wench:' / So, rushing in the bowels of the French, / He left me proudly, as unworthy fight.

Once I met him, and I said: "You virgin youth, be beaten by a virgin." But with proud, majestic, lofty scorn he answered: "Young Talbot wasn't born to be the spoil of a loose wench." So, rushing into the thick of the French, he proudly left me, as not worth fighting.
Doubtless he would have made a noble knight: / See, where he lies inhearsed in the arms / Of the most bloody nurser of his harms!
No doubt he would have made a noble knight. Look how he lies coffined in the arms of the man who bloodily bred his ruin!
Hew them to pieces, hack their bones asunder, / Whose life was England's glory, Gallia's wonder.
Hack them to pieces, chop their bones apart, whose lives were England's glory and France's wonder.
O, no, forbear! for that which we have fled / During the life, let us not wrong it dead.
Oh no, stop! What we ran from while they lived, let's not wrong now they're dead.
Herald, conduct me to the Dauphin's tent, / To know who hath obtain'd the glory of the day.
Herald, take me to the Dauphin's tent to find out who has won the glory of the day.
On what submissive message art thou sent?
What message of surrender have you been sent with?
Submission, Dauphin! 'tis a mere French word; / We English warriors wot not what it means. / I come to know what prisoners thou hast ta'en, / And to survey the bodies of the dead.
Surrender, Dauphin! That's purely a French word; we English soldiers don't know what it means. I've come to find out what prisoners you have taken and to look at the bodies of the dead.
For prisoners ask'st thou? hell our prison is. / But tell me whom thou seek'st.
You're asking about prisoners? Hell is our prison. But tell me whom you're looking for.

But where's the great Alcides of the field, / Valiant Lord Talbot, Earl of Shrewsbury, / Created for his rare success in arms, / Great Earl of Washford, Waterford, and Valence; / Lord Talbot of Goodrig and Urchinfield, / Lord Strange of Blackmere, Lord Verdun of Alton, / Lord Cromwell of Wingfield, Lord Furnival of Sheffield, / The thrice-victorious Lord of Falconbridge; / Knight of the noble order of Saint George, / Worthy Saint Michael, and the Golden Fleece; / Great marshal to Henry the Sixth / Of all his wars within the realm of France?

Where's the great Hercules of the battlefield, brave Lord Talbot, Earl of Shrewsbury, made great Earl of Wexford, Waterford and Valence for his outstanding success in war; Lord Talbot of Goodrich and Urchinfield, Lord Strange of Blackmere, Lord Verdun of Alton, Lord Cromwell of Wingfield, Lord Furnival of Sheffield, the three-times victorious Lord of Falconbridge; Knight of the noble Order of Saint George, worthy Saint Michael and the Golden Fleece; great Marshal to Henry the Sixth in all his wars in France?

Here's a silly stately style indeed! / The Turk, that two and fifty kingdoms hath, / Writes not so tedious a style as this. / Him that thou magnifiest with all these titles / Stinking and fly-blown lies here at our feet.

That's a ridiculously grand list of titles! The Sultan of Turkey, who has fifty-two kingdoms, doesn't write such a long-winded list. The man you glorify with all these titles lies here at our feet, stinking and covered in flies.

Is Talbot slain, the Frenchman's only scourge, / Your kingdom's terror and black Nemesis? / O, were mine eye-balls into bullets turn'd, / That I in rage might shoot them at your faces! / O, that I could but can these dead to life! / It were enough to fright the realm of France: / Were but his picture left amongst you here, / It would amaze the proudest of you all. / Give me their bodies, that I may bear them hence / And give them burial as beseems their worth.

Is Talbot killed, the only scourge of the French, your kingdom's terror and dark goddess of vengeance? Oh, if only my eyeballs were turned into bullets so that I could shoot them in rage at your faces! Oh, if only I could call these dead back to life! It would be enough to frighten the whole of France. If only his portrait were left here among you, it would terrify the proudest of you. Give me their bodies, so I can carry them away and bury them as their worth deserves.
I think this upstart is old Talbot's ghost, / He speaks with such a proud commanding spirit, / For God's sake, let him have 'em; to keep them here, / They would but stink, and putrify the air.
I think this upstart is old Talbot's ghost, he speaks with such a proud, commanding spirit. For God's sake, let him have them; if we keep them here, they'd only stink and rot the air.
I'll bear them hence; but from their ashes shall be / rear'd / A phoenix that shall make all France afeard.
I'll carry them away; but from their ashes a phoenix will rise that will make all France afraid.
So we be rid of them, do with 'em what thou wilt. / And now to Paris, in this conquering vein: / All will be ours, now bloody Talbot's slain.
As long as we're rid of them, do what you like with them. And now to Paris, while we're on a winning streak. Everything will be ours now bloody Talbot is dead.
Have you perused the letters from the pope, / The emperor, and the Earl of Armagnac?
Have you read the letters from the Pope, the Emperor and the Earl of Armagnac?
I have, my lord: and their intent is this: / They humbly sue unto your excellence / To have a godly peace concluded of / Between the realms of England and of France.
I have, my lord, and this is what they want: they humbly ask your Excellency to agree a holy peace between the kingdoms of England and France.
How doth your grace affect their motion?
What does your Grace think of their proposal?
Well, my good lord; and as the only means / To stop effusion of our Christian blood / And stablish quietness on every side.
I like it, my good lord, as the only way to stop the spilling of Christian blood and bring peace on every side.
Aye, marry, uncle; for I always thought / It was both impious and unnatural / That such immanity and bloody strife / Should reign among professors of one faith.
Yes indeed, uncle; for I always thought it was both wicked and unnatural that such savagery and bloody fighting should rule among people of the same faith.

Beside, my lord, the sooner to effect / And surer bind this knot of amity, / The Earl of Armagnac, near knit to Charles, / A man of great authority in France, / Proffers his only daughter to your grace / In marriage, with a large and sumptuous dowry.

Besides, my lord, to bring about this bond of friendship faster and tie it more securely, the Earl of Armagnac, closely related to Charles and a man of great power in France, offers your Grace his only daughter in marriage, with a large and rich dowry.

Marriage, uncle! alas, my years are young! / And fitter is my study and my books / Than wanton dalliance with a paramour. / Yet call the ambassadors; and, as you please, / So let them have their answers every one: / I shall be well content with any choice / Tends to God's glory and my country's weal.

Marriage, uncle! Alas, I'm young! My studies and my books suit me better than playful flirting with a sweetheart. Still, call the ambassadors and give them each whatever answer you think best. I'll be happy with any choice that serves God's glory and my country's good.

What! is my Lord of Winchester install'd / And call'd unto a cardinal's degree? / Then I perceive that will be verified / Henry the Fifth did sometime prophesy, / 'If once he come to be a cardinal, / He'll make his cap co-equal with the crown.'

What! Has my Lord of Winchester been installed and promoted to cardinal? Then I see what Henry the Fifth once prophesied will come true: "If he ever becomes a cardinal, he'll make his hat equal to the crown."

My lords ambassadors, your several suits / Have been consider'd and debated on. / Your purpose is both good and reasonable; / And therefore are we certainly resolved / To draw conditions of a friendly peace; / Which by my Lord of Winchester we mean / Shall be transported presently to France.

My lords ambassadors, your various requests have been considered and debated. Your aim is both good and reasonable, so we have firmly decided to draw up terms for a friendly peace, which we intend my Lord of Winchester to take to France at once.

And for the proffer of my lord your master, / I have inform'd his highness so at large, / As liking of the lady's virtuous gifts, / Her beauty and the value of her dower, / He doth intend she shall be England's Queen.
And as for your master's offer, I have told his Highness about it in full, and liking the lady's virtues, her beauty and the value of her dowry, he intends her to be England's Queen.

In argument and proof of which contract, / Bear her this jewel, pledge of my affection. / And so, my lord protector, see them guarded / And safely brought to Dover; where inshipp'd, / Commit them to the fortune of the sea.

As a sign and proof of this agreement, take her this jewel, a pledge of my love. And so, Lord Protector, see them escorted and brought safely to Dover, and there, once they've boarded, trust them to the fortune of the sea.
Stay my lord legate: you shall first receive / The sum of money which I promised / Should be deliver'd to his holiness / For clothing me in these grave ornaments.
Wait, my Lord Legate. First you'll receive the sum of money I promised to deliver to his Holiness for dressing me in these solemn robes.
I will attend upon your lordship's leisure.
I'll wait until your lordship is ready.

[Aside] Now Winchester will not submit, I trow, / Or be inferior to the proudest peer. / Humphrey of Gloucester, thou shalt well perceive / That neither in birth or for authority, / The bishop will be overborne by thee: / I'll either make thee stoop and bend thy knee, / Or sack this country with a mutiny.

(Aside) Now I'm sure Winchester won't submit to or be lower than the proudest lord. Humphrey of Gloucester, you'll see clearly that the bishop won't be overpowered by you, either in birth or in authority. I'll either make you bow and bend your knee or wreck this country with a rebellion.
These news, my lords, may cheer our drooping spirits: / 'Tis said the stout Parisians do revolt / And turn again unto the warlike French.
This news, my lords, may cheer up our drooping spirits: they say the bold Parisians are rebelling and coming back to the warlike French.
Then march to Paris, royal Charles of France, / And keep not back your powers in dalliance.
Then march to Paris, royal Charles of France, and don't hold your forces back in idleness.
Peace be amongst them, if they turn to us; / Else, ruin combat with their palaces!
Peace be with them, if they come back to us; otherwise, may ruin fight with their palaces!
Success unto our valiant general, / And happiness to his accomplices!
Success to our brave general, and happiness to his allies!
What tidings send our scouts? I prithee, speak.
What news do our scouts send? Please speak.
The English army, that divided was / Into two parties, is now conjoin'd in one, / And means to give you battle presently.
The English army, which was divided into two parts, has now joined into one and means to give you battle at once.
Somewhat too sudden, sirs, the warning is; / But we will presently provide for them.
The warning is rather sudden, sirs, but we'll get ready for them at once.
I trust the ghost of Talbot is not there: / Now he is gone, my lord, you need not fear.
I'm sure the ghost of Talbot isn't there. Now he's gone, my lord, you needn't be afraid.
Of all base passions, fear is most accursed. / Command the conquest, Charles, it shall be thine, / Let Henry fret and all the world repine.
Of all low feelings, fear is the most cursed. Order the victory, Charles, and it will be yours. Let Henry fret and the whole world complain.
Then on, my lords; and France be fortunate!
Then forward, my lords, and good fortune to France!

The regent conquers, and the Frenchmen fly. / Now help, ye charming spells and periapts; / And ye choice spirits that admonish me, / And give me signs of future accidents. [Thunder] / You speedy helpers, that are substitutes / Under the lordly monarch of the north, / Appear and aid me in this enterprise.

The Regent is winning, and the French are running away. Now help me, you magic spells and charms, and you chosen spirits who advise me and give me signs of future events! (Thunder) You quick helpers who serve under the lordly king of the north, appear and help me in this enterprise.

This speedy and quick appearance argues proof / Of your accustom'd diligence to me. / Now, ye familiar spirits, that are cull'd / Out of the powerful regions under earth, / Help me this once, that France may get the field.
This quick appearance proves your usual devotion to me. Now, you familiar spirits picked from the powerful regions under the earth, help me this once so that France may win the battle.
O, hold me not with silence over-long! / Where I was wont to feed you with my blood, / I'll lop a member off and give it you / In earnest of a further benefit, / So you do condescend to help me now.
Oh, don't keep me waiting in silence too long! Where I used to feed you with my blood, I'll cut off a limb and give it to you as a down payment on a further reward, if you'll agree to help me now.
No hope to have redress? My body shall / Pay recompense, if you will grant my suit.
No hope of help? My body will pay you, if you'll grant my request.
Cannot my body nor blood-sacrifice / Entreat you to your wonted furtherance? / Then take my soul, my body, soul and all, / Before that England give the French the foil.
Can't my body or my blood sacrifice persuade you to help me as usual? Then take my soul, my body, soul and all, before England defeats the French.

See, they forsake me! Now the time is come / That France must vail her lofty-plumed crest, / And let her head fall into England's lap. / My ancient incantations are too weak, / And hell too strong for me to buckle with: / Now, France, thy glory droopeth to the dust.

Look, they're abandoning me! Now the time has come when France must lower her proud, plumed helmet and let her head fall into England's lap. My old spells are too weak, and hell is too strong for me to wrestle with. Now, France, your glory droops into the dust.

Damsel of France, I think I have you fast: / Unchain your spirits now with spelling charms, / And try if they can gain your liberty. / A goodly prize, fit for the devil's grace! / See, how the ugly witch doth bend her brows, / As if with Circe she would change my shape!

Girl of France, I think I've got you tight. Now unleash your spirits with your spells and see if they can win your freedom. A fine prize, fit for the devil's grace! See how the ugly witch frowns, as if she would change my shape like Circe!
Chang'd to a worser shape thou canst not be.
You can't be changed into a worse shape.
O, Charles the Dauphin is a proper man; / No shape but his can please your dainty eye.
Oh, Charles the Dauphin is a handsome man; no shape but his can please your fussy eye.
A plaguing mischief light on Charles and thee! / And may ye both be suddenly surprised / By bloody hands, in sleeping on your beds!
May a plague of trouble fall on Charles and you! And may you both be surprised by murderers while you sleep in your beds!
Fell banning hag; enchantress, hold thy tongue!
Cruel cursing hag! Witch, hold your tongue!
I prithee, give me leave to curse awhile.
Please let me curse a while.
Curse, miscreant, when thou comest to the stake.
Curse, villain, when you come to the stake.
Be what thou wilt, thou art my prisoner.
Be who you like, you are my prisoner.

O fairest beauty, do not fear nor fly! / For I will touch thee but with reverent hands; / I kiss these fingers for eternal peace, / And lay them gently on thy tender side. / Who art thou? say, that I may honor thee.

Oh, fairest beauty, don't be afraid or run away! I'll only touch you with respectful hands. I kiss these fingers as a sign of everlasting peace and lay them gently at your side. Who are you? Tell me, so I can honour you.
Margaret my name, and daughter to a king, / The King of Naples, whosoe'er thou art.
My name is Margaret, and I'm a king's daughter, the King of Naples, whoever you are.

An earl I am, and Suffolk am I call'd. / Be not offended, nature's miracle, / Thou art allotted to be ta'en by me. / So doth the swan her downy cygnets save, / Keeping them prisoner underneath her wings. / Yet, if this servile usage once offend, / Go and be free again as Suffolk's friend.

I am an earl, and my name is Suffolk. Don't be offended, miracle of nature; it's your lot to be taken by me. That's how the swan protects her fluffy cygnets, keeping them prisoner under her wings. Still, if this treatment as a captive offends you, go and be free again as Suffolk's friend.

O, stay! I have no power to let her pass; / My hand would free her, but my heart says no. / As plays the sun upon the glassy streams, / Twinkling another counterfeited beam, / So seems this gorgeous beauty to mine eyes. / Fain would I woo her, yet I dare not speak: / I'll call for pen and ink, and write my mind. / Fie, de la Pole! disable not thyself; / Hast not a tongue? is she not here? / Wilt thou be daunted at a woman's sight? / Aye, beauty's princely majesty is such, / Confounds the tongue and makes the senses rough.

Oh, stay! I don't have the power to let her go. My hand would free her, but my heart says no. As the sun plays on glassy streams, sparkling with a second, reflected beam, so this gorgeous beauty seems to my eyes. I'd like to woo her, but I don't dare speak. I'll call for pen and ink and write my thoughts. Shame, de la Pole! Don't belittle yourself. Haven't you got a tongue? Isn't she here? Will you be scared by the sight of a woman? Yes, beauty's princely majesty is such that it ties the tongue and dulls the senses.
Say, Earl of Suffolk,—if thy name be so— / What ransom must I pay before I pass? / For I perceive I am thy prisoner.
Tell me, Earl of Suffolk, if that's your name, what ransom must I pay before I can go? For I see I am your prisoner.
How canst thou tell she will deny thy suit, / Before thou make a trial of her love?
(Aside) How can you tell she'll reject your suit before you've tested her love?
Why speak'st thou not? what ransom must I pay?
Why don't you speak? What ransom must I pay?
She's beautiful and therefore to be woo'd; / She is a woman, therefore to be won.
(Aside) She's beautiful, and so she should be wooed; she's a woman, and so she can be won.
Wilt thou accept of ransom? yea, or no.
Will you accept a ransom? Yes or no?
Fond man, remember that thou hast a wife; / Then how can Margaret be thy paramour?
(Aside) Foolish man, remember you have a wife. So how can Margaret be your lover?
I were best leave him, for he will not hear.
I'd better leave him, for he won't listen.
There all is marr'd; there lies a cooling card.
(Aside) That spoils everything; that's the card that cools my hopes.
He talks at random; sure, the man is mad.
He's rambling; the man must be mad.
And yet a dispensation may be had.
(Aside) And yet a special permission from the Church could be had.
And yet I would that you would answer me.
And yet I wish you'd answer me.
I'll win this Lady Margaret. For whom? / Why, for my king; tush, that 's a wooden thing!
(Aside) I'll win this Lady Margaret. For whom? Why, for my king. Pooh, that's a wooden idea!
He talks of wood: it is some carpenter.
He's talking about wood; he must be a carpenter.

Yet so my fancy may be satisfied, / And peace established between these realms. / But there remains a scruple in that too; / For though her father be the King of Naples, / Duke of Anjou and Maine, yet is he poor, / And our nobility will scorn the match.

(Aside) Yet that way my desire may be satisfied and peace made between these kingdoms. But there's a problem with that too: though her father is King of Naples and Duke of Anjou and Maine, he's poor, and our nobles will scorn the match.
Hear ye, captain, are you not at leisure?
Listen, captain, aren't you free to talk?
It shall be so, disdain they ne'er so much: / Henry is youthful and will quickly yield. / Madam, I have a secret to reveal.
(Aside) It shall be so, however much they scorn it. Henry is young and will quickly give in. (To her) Madam, I have a secret to tell you.
What though I be enthrall'd? he seems a knight, / And will not any way dishonor me.
(Aside) What if I am a prisoner? He seems to be a knight and won't dishonour me in any way.
Lady, vouchsafe to listen what I say.
Lady, be good enough to listen to what I say.
Perhaps I shall be rescued by the French; / And then I need not crave his courtesy.
(Aside) Perhaps the French will rescue me, and then I won't need to beg for his courtesy.
Sweet madam, give me hearing in a cause—
Sweet madam, hear me out on a matter—
Tush! women have been captivate ere now.
(Aside) Pooh! Women have been taken captive before now.
Lady, why do you talk like that?
I cry you mercy, 'tis but Quid for Quo.
I beg your pardon; it's only tit for tat.
Say, gentle princess, would you not suppose / Your bondage happy, to be made a queen?
Tell me, gentle princess, wouldn't you think your captivity happy if it made you a queen?
To be a queen in bondage is more vile / Than is a slave in base servility; / For princes should be free.
To be a queen in captivity is worse than to be a slave in low servitude, for royalty should be free.
And so shall you, / If happy England's royal king be free.
And so you shall be, if happy England's royal king is free.
Why, what concerns his freedom unto me?
Why, what has his freedom to do with me?
I'll undertake to make thee Henry's queen, / To put a golden scepter in thy hand / And set a precious crown upon thy head, / If thou wilt condescend to be my—
I'll undertake to make you Henry's queen, to put a golden sceptre in your hand and set a precious crown on your head, if you'll agree to be my—
I am unworthy to be Henry's wife.
I'm not worthy to be Henry's wife.
No, gentle madam; I unworthy am / To woo so fair a dame to be his wife, / And have no portion in the choice myself. / How say you, madam, are ye so content?
No, gentle madam; I'm unworthy to woo so fair a lady to be his wife and have no share in the choice myself. What do you say, madam? Do you agree?
An if my father please, I am content.
If my father agrees, I agree.
Then call our captain and our colors forth. / And, madam, at your father's castle walls / We'll crave a parley, to confer with him.
Then call out our captains and our flags. And, madam, we'll ask for a parley at your father's castle walls to talk with him.
See, Reignier, see, thy daughter prisoner!
Look, Reignier, look, your daughter is a prisoner!
Suffolk, what remedy? / I am a soldier, and unapt to weep, / Or to exclaim on fortune's fickleness.
Suffolk, what can be done? I'm a soldier and not inclined to weep or rail against fortune's fickleness.

Yes, there is remedy enough, my lord: / Consent, and for thy honor give consent, / Thy daughter shall be wedded to my king; / Whom I with pain have woo'd and won thereto; / And this her easy-held imprisonment / Hath gain'd thy daughter princely liberty.

Yes, there's plenty to be done, my lord. Agree, and for your honour agree, that your daughter will marry my king, whom I've wooed and won to it with some effort; and this easy imprisonment of hers has won your daughter royal freedom.
Does Suffolk mean what he says?
Fair Margaret knows / That Suffolk doth not flatter, face, or feign.
Fair Margaret knows that Suffolk doesn't flatter, pretend or lie.
Upon thy princely warrant, I descend / To give thee answer of thy just demand.
On your princely word, I'll come down to give you an answer to your fair request.
And here I will expect thy coming.
And I'll wait here for you to come.
Welcome, brave earl, into our territories: / Command in Anjou what your honor pleases.
Welcome, brave Earl, to our lands. Command whatever your lordship pleases in Anjou.
Thanks, Reignier, happy for so sweet a child, / Fit to be made companion with a king: / What answer makes your grace unto my suit?
Thank you, Reignier, lucky to have so sweet a child, fit to be a king's partner. What answer does your Grace give to my proposal?

Since thou dost deign to woo her little worth / To be the princely bride of such a lord; / Upon condition I may quietly / Enjoy mine own, the country Maine and Anjou, / Free from oppression or the stroke of war, / My daughter shall be Henry's, if he please.

Since you are good enough to woo her, of little worth as she is, to be the royal bride of such a lord: on condition that I may peacefully enjoy my own lands, the counties of Maine and Anjou, free from oppression and the blows of war, my daughter shall be Henry's, if he wishes.
That is her ransom; I deliver her; / And those two counties I will undertake / Your Grace shall well and quietly enjoy.
That's her ransom. I release her, and I promise your Grace that you'll enjoy those two counties fully and in peace.
And I again, in Henry's royal name, / As deputy unto that gracious king, / Give thee her hand, for sign of plighted faith.
And I in return, in Henry's royal name, as deputy for that gracious king, give you her hand as a sign of her promise.

Reignier of France, I give thee kingly thanks, / Because this is in traffic of a king. / [Aside] And yet, methinks, I could be well content / To be mine own attorney in this case. / I'll over then to England with this news, / And make this marriage to be solemnized. / So, farewell, Reignier; set this diamond safe / In golden palaces, as it becomes.

Reignier of France, I give you royal thanks, since this is a king's business. (Aside) And yet I think I'd be very happy to act on my own behalf in this case. (Aloud) I'll go over to England with this news and arrange for this marriage to be celebrated. So goodbye, Reignier; keep this diamond safe in golden palaces, as it deserves.
I do embrace thee as I would embrace / The Christian prince, King Henry, were he here.
I embrace you as I would embrace the Christian prince, King Henry, if he were here.
Farewell, my lord: good wishes, praise and prayers. / Shall Suffolk ever have of Margaret. [Going]
Goodbye, my lord. Suffolk will always have Margaret's good wishes, praise and prayers. (Going)
Farewell, sweet madam: but hark you, Margaret; / No princely commendations to my king?
Goodbye, sweet madam. But listen, Margaret: no royal greetings for my king?
Such commendations as becomes a maid, / A virgin and his servant, say to him.
Tell him such greetings as suit a girl, a virgin and his servant.
Words sweetly placed and modestly directed. / But, madam, I must trouble you again; / No loving token to his majesty?
Words sweetly put and modestly aimed. But, madam, I must trouble you again: no love token for his Majesty?
Yes, my good lord, a pure unspotted heart, / Never yet taint with love, I send the king.
Yes, my good lord: I send the King a pure, unspotted heart, never yet touched by love.
That for thyself: I will not so presume / To send such peevish tokens to a king.
That's for you. I won't be so bold as to send such silly tokens to a king.

O, wert thou for myself! But, Suffolk, stay; / Thou mayst not wander in that labyrinth; / There Minotaurs and ugly treasons lurk. / Solicit Henry with her wondrous praise: / Bethink thee on her virtues that surmount, / And natural graces that extinguish art; / Repeat their semblance often on the seas, / That, when thou comest to kneel at Henry's feet, / Thou mayst bereave him of his wits with wonder.

Oh, if only you were for me! But, Suffolk, stop: you mustn't wander into that maze. Monsters and ugly treasons lurk there. Woo Henry with wonderful praise of her. Think about her outstanding virtues and natural graces that put art to shame. Go over their image often on the voyage, so that when you come to kneel at Henry's feet, you can rob him of his wits with wonder.
Bring forth that sorceress condemn'd to burn.
Bring out that witch who is condemned to burn.

Ah, Joan, this kills thy father's heart outright! / Have I sought every country far and near, / And now it is my chance to find thee out, / Must I behold thy timeless cruel death? / Ah, Joan, sweet daughter Joan, I'll die with thee!

Ah, Joan, this breaks your father's heart completely! Have I searched every land far and near, and now that I happen to find you, must I see your early, cruel death? Ah, Joan, sweet daughter Joan, I'll die with you!
Decrepit miser! base ignoble wretch! / I am descended of a gentler blood: / Thou art no father nor no friend of mine.
Broken-down old wretch! Low, common creature! I'm descended from nobler blood. You are no father or friend of mine.
Out, out! My lords, as please you, 'tis not so; / I did beget her, all the parish knows. / Her mother liveth yet, can testify / She was the first fruit of my bachelorship.
No, no! My lords, if you please, it isn't so. I fathered her; the whole parish knows it. Her mother is still alive and can testify she was my first child after I married.
Graceless! wilt thou deny thy parentage?
Shameless girl! Will you deny your parents?
This argues what her kind of life hath been, / Wicked and vile; and so her death concludes.
This shows what kind of life she's led, wicked and vile; and her death ends it the same way.
Fie, Joan, that thou wilt be so obstacle! / God knows thou art a collop of my flesh; / And for thy sake have I shed many a tear: / Deny me not, I prithee, gentle Joan.
Shame, Joan, that you are so stubborn! God knows you are a piece of my flesh, and I've shed many tears for you. Please don't deny me, gentle Joan.
Peasant, avaunt! You have suborn'd this man, / Of purpose to obscure my noble birth.
Away, peasant! (To the English) You have bribed this man to hide my noble birth.

'Tis true, I gave a noble to the priest / The morn that I was wedded to her mother. / Kneel down and take my blessing, good my girl. / Wilt thou not stoop? Now cursed be the time / Of thy nativity! I would the milk / Thy mother gave thee when thou suck'dst her breast, / Had been a little ratsbane for thy sake! / Or else, when thou didst keep my lambs a-field, / I wish some ravenous wolf had eaten thee! / Dost thou deny thy father, cursed drab? / O, burn her, burn her! hanging is too good.

It's true, I gave the priest a coin the morning I married her mother. Kneel down and take my blessing, my good girl. Won't you bow? Then cursed be the hour you were born! I wish the milk your mother gave you when you sucked her breast had been rat poison, for your sake! Or else, when you looked after my lambs in the field, I wish some hungry wolf had eaten you! Do you deny your father, cursed slut? Oh, burn her, burn her! Hanging's too good for her.
Take her away; for she hath lived too long, / To fill the world with vicious qualities.
Take her away, for she has lived too long, filling the world with wickedness.

First, let me tell you whom you have condemn'd: / Not me begotten of a shepherd swain, / But issued from the progeny of kings; / Virtuous and holy; chosen from above, / By inspiration of celestial grace, / To work exceeding miracles on earth. / I never had to do with wicked spirits: / But you, that are polluted with your lusts, / Stain'd with the guiltless blood of innocents, / Corrupt and tainted with a thousand vices, / Because you want the grace that others have, / You judge it straight a thing impossible / To compass wonders but by help of devils. / No, misconceived! Joan of Arc hath been / A virgin from her tender infancy, / Chaste and immaculate in very thought; / Whose maiden blood, thus rigorously effused, / Will cry for vengeance at the gates of heaven.

First let me tell you whom you have condemned: not someone fathered by a shepherd peasant, but one descended from kings; virtuous and holy, chosen from above by the inspiration of heavenly grace to work great miracles on earth. I never had anything to do with evil spirits. But you, who are filthy with your lusts, stained with the blameless blood of innocent people, corrupt and infected with a thousand vices, because you lack the grace others have, immediately judge it impossible to perform wonders except with the help of devils. No, you are mistaken! Joan of Arc has been a virgin from her earliest childhood, chaste and pure even in thought, and her virgin blood, cruelly spilled like this, will cry out for vengeance at the gates of heaven.
Aye, aye: away with her to execution!
Yes, yes. Away with her to execution!
And hark ye, sirs; because she is a maid, / Spare for no faggots, let there be enow: / Place barrels of pitch upon the fatal stake, / That so her torture may be shortened.
And listen, men: since she's a virgin, don't hold back on the firewood; let there be plenty. Put barrels of tar on the fatal stake so that her suffering may be shortened.

Will nothing turn your unrelenting hearts? / Then, Joan, discover thine infirmity, / That warranteth by law to be thy privilege. / I am with child, ye bloody homicides: / Murder not then the fruit within my womb, / Although ye hale me to a violent death.

Will nothing soften your merciless hearts? Then, Joan, reveal your condition, which by law gives you protection. I am pregnant, you bloody murderers. So don't murder the fruit in my womb, even if you drag me to a violent death.
Now heaven forfend! the holy maid with child!
Heaven forbid! The holy virgin pregnant!
The greatest miracle that e'er ye wrought: / Is all your strict preciseness come to this?
The greatest miracle you ever performed! Has all your strict purity come to this?
She and the Dauphin have been juggling: / I did imagine what would be her refuge.
She and the Dauphin have been up to tricks. I suspected what her last resort would be.
Well, go to; we'll have no bastards live; / Especially since Charles must father it.
Well, come on; we won't let any bastards live, especially since Charles must be the father.
You are deceived; my child is none of his: / It was Alencon that enjoy'd my love.
You're wrong; my child isn't his. It was Alencon who enjoyed my love.
Alencon! that notorious Machiavel! / It dies, an if it had a thousand lives.
Alencon! That notorious schemer! It dies, if it had a thousand lives.
O, give me leave, I have deluded you: / 'Twas neither Charles nor yet the duke I named, / But Reignier, king of Naples, that prevail'd.
Oh, let me correct myself; I misled you. It was neither Charles nor the Duke I named, but Reignier, King of Naples, who won me.
A married man! that's most intolerable.
A married man! That's completely intolerable.
Why, here's a girl! I think she knows not well / There were so many, whom she may accuse.
Why, what a girl! I don't think she knows for sure, there were so many she could accuse.
It's sign she hath been liberal and free.
It's a sign she's been generous and free with herself.
And yet, forsooth, she is a virgin pure. / Strumpet, thy words condemn thy brat and thee: / Use no entreaty, for it is in vain.
And yet, if you please, she's a pure virgin. Whore, your own words condemn your brat and you. Don't plead; it's useless.

Then lead me hence; with whom I leave my curse: / May never glorious sun reflex his beams / Upon the country where you make abode: / But darkness and the gloomy shade of death / Environ you, till mischief and despair / Drive you to break your necks or hang yourselves!

Then lead me away; I leave you my curse. May the glorious sun never shine its rays on the country where you live, but may darkness and the gloomy shadow of death surround you, until misfortune and despair drive you to break your necks or hang yourselves!
Break thou in pieces and consume to ashes, / Thou foul accursed minister of hell!
Break into pieces and burn to ashes, you foul, cursed servant of hell!

Lord regent, I do greet your excellence / With letters of commission from the king. / For know, my lords, the states of Christendom, / Moved with remorse of these outrageous broils, / Have earnestly implored a general peace / Betwixt our nation and the aspiring French; / And here at hand the Dauphin and his train / Approacheth, to confer about some matter.

Lord Regent, I greet your Excellency with a commission from the King. For you should know, my lords, that the states of Christendom, moved by pity for these outrageous wars, have earnestly begged for a general peace between our nation and the ambitious French; and the Dauphin and his followers are approaching close by to discuss terms.

Is all our travail turn'd to this effect? / After the slaughter of so many peers, / So many captains, gentlemen and soldiers, / That in this quarrel have been overthrown, / And sold their bodies for their country's benefit, / Shall we at last conclude effeminate peace? / Have we not lost most part of all the towns, / By treason, falsehood, and by treachery, / Our great progenitors had conquered? / O, Warwick, Warwick! I foresee with grief / The utter loss of all the realm of France.

Has all our labour come to this? After the slaughter of so many lords, captains, gentlemen and soldiers, who have fallen in this quarrel and given their bodies for their country's good, are we going to agree to a weak, womanish peace at last? Haven't we lost most of the towns our great ancestors conquered, through treason, lies and treachery? Oh, Warwick, Warwick! I foresee with grief the complete loss of the whole kingdom of France.
Be patient, York: if we conclude / a peace, / It shall be with such strict and severe covenants / As little shall the Frenchmen gain thereby.
Be patient, York. If we make peace, it will be with such strict and harsh terms that the French will gain little from it.
Since, lords of England, it is thus agreed / That peaceful truce shall be proclaim'd in France, / We come to be informed by yourselves / What the conditions of that league must be.
Lords of England, since it is agreed that a peaceful truce will be proclaimed in France, we have come to hear from you what the terms of that agreement must be.
Speak, Winchester; for boiling choler chokes / The hollow passage of my poison'd voice, / By sight of these our baleful enemies.
Speak, Winchester; for boiling anger at the sight of these hateful enemies of ours chokes the hollow passage of my poisoned voice.

Charles, and the rest, it is enacted thus: / That, in regard King Henry gives consent, / Of mere compassion and of lenity, / To ease your country of distressful war, / And suffer you to breathe in fruitful peace, / You shall become true liegemen to his crown: / And, Charles, upon condition thou wilt swear / To pay him tribute and submit thyself, / Thou shalt be placed as viceroy under him, / And still enjoy the regal dignity.

Charles, and the rest of you, these are the terms: since King Henry agrees, out of pure pity and mercy, to free your country from painful war and let you breathe in fruitful peace, you will become loyal subjects of his crown. And, Charles, on condition that you swear to pay him tribute and submit to him, you'll be made viceroy under him and still enjoy royal rank.
Must he be then as shadow of himself? / Adorn his temples with a coronet, / And yet, in substance and authority, / Retain but privilege of a private man? / This proffer is absurd and reasonless.
Must he be a shadow of himself, then? Decorate his head with a crown, and yet, in reality and power, keep only the rights of a private man? This offer is absurd and unreasonable.

'Tis known already that I am possess'd / With more than half the Gallian territories, / And therein reverenced for their lawful king: / Shall I, for lucre of the rest unvanquish'd, / Detract so much from that prerogative, / As to be call'd but viceroy of the whole? / No, lord ambassador, I'll rather keep / That which I have than, coveting for more, / Be cast from possibility of all.

It's well known that I already hold more than half the lands of France and am honoured there as their lawful king. Shall I, for the sake of gaining the rest that's still unconquered, give up so much of that royal right as to be called only viceroy of the whole? No, Lord Ambassador; I'd rather keep what I have than, by grasping for more, lose the chance of everything.

Insulting Charles! hast thou by secret means / Used intercession to obtain a league, / And, now the matter grows to compromise, / Stand'st thou aloof upon comparison? / Either accept the title thou usurp'st, / Of benefit proceeding from our king / And not of any challenge of desert, / Or we will plague thee with incessant wars.

Insolent Charles! Have you secretly used go-betweens to get a treaty, and now that it comes to an agreement, do you hold back and quibble over terms? Either accept the title you have stolen as a favour from our king, and not as something you have earned, or we'll torment you with endless wars.
My lord, you do not well in obstinacy / To cavil in the course of this contract: / If once it be neglected, ten to one / We shall not find like opportunity.
My lord, you're wrong to be stubborn and pick holes in this agreement. If we once let it slip, it's ten to one we won't get another chance like it.

To say the truth, it is your policy / To save your subjects from such massacre / And ruthless slaughters as are daily seen, / By our proceeding in hostility; / And therefore take this compact of a truce, / Although you break it when your pleasure serves.

To tell the truth, it's good policy to save your subjects from the massacres and merciless slaughter we see every day as we keep on fighting. So take this treaty of truce, even if you break it when it suits you.
How say'st thou, Charles? shall our condition stand?
What do you say, Charles? Shall our terms stand?
It shall; / Only reserv'd, you claim no interest / In any of our towns of garrison.
They shall, on the one condition that you claim no rights in any of our garrison towns.

Then swear allegiance to his majesty, / As thou art knight, never to disobey / Nor be rebellious to the crown of England / Thou, nor thy nobles, to the crown of England. / So, now dismiss your army when ye please; / Hang up your ensigns, let your drums be still, / For here we entertain a solemn peace.

Then swear allegiance to his Majesty: as you are a knight, never to disobey or rebel against the crown of England, neither you nor your nobles. So, now disband your army when you like; hang up your flags and silence your drums, for here we make a solemn peace.

Your wondrous rare description, noble earl, / Of beauteous Margaret hath astonish'd me. / Her virtues graced with external gifts / Do breed love's settled passions in my heart: / And like as rigor of tempestuous gusts / Provokes the mightiest hulk against the tide, / So am I driven by breath of her renown, / Either to suffer shipwreck or arrive / Where I may have fruition of her love.

Your wonderful description of beautiful Margaret, noble Earl, has amazed me. Her virtues, graced with outward beauty, plant love's firm passion in my heart. And just as the force of stormy winds drives the mightiest ship against the tide, so I am driven by the breath of her fame either to suffer shipwreck or to arrive where I can enjoy her love.

Tush, my good lord, this superficial tale / Is but a preface of her worthy praise; / The chief perfections of that lovely dame, / Had I sufficient skill to utter them, / Would make a volume of enticing lines, / Able to ravish any dull conceit: / And, which is more, she is not so divine, / So full-replete with choice of all delights, / But with as humble lowliness of mind / She is content to be at your command; / Command, I mean, of virtuous intents, / To love and honor Henry as her lord.

Pooh, my good lord, this surface account is only an introduction to the praise she deserves. The chief perfections of that lovely lady, if I had the skill to describe them, would fill a book of enchanting lines able to delight the dullest mind. And what's more, she isn't so divine, so full of every choice delight, that she isn't content, with humble modesty, to be at your command: command, I mean, in virtuous matters, to love and honour Henry as her lord.
And otherwise will Henry ne'er presume. / Therefore, my lord protector, give consent / That Margaret may be England's royal queen.
And Henry will never presume to ask otherwise. So, Lord Protector, give your consent for Margaret to be England's royal queen.

So should I give consent to flatter sin. / You know, my lord, your highness is betroth'd / Unto another lady of esteem: / How shall we then dispense with that contract, / And not deface your honor with reproach?
That would be agreeing to flatter sin. You know, my lord, your Highness is engaged to another lady of high rank. How can we set aside that contract without staining your honour with disgrace?

As doth a ruler with unlawful oaths; / Or one that, at a triumph having vow'd / To try his strength, forsaketh yet the lists / By reason of his adversary's odds: / A poor earl's daughter is unequal odds, / And therefore may be broke without offense.

The way a ruler sets aside unlawful oaths; or like someone who has vowed to test his strength at a tournament but then leaves the lists because his opponent is so outclassed. A poor earl's daughter is an unequal match, and so it can be broken off without offence.
Why, what, I pray, is Margaret more than that? / Her father is no better than an earl, / Although in glorious titles he excel.
Why, what is Margaret more than that, I'd like to know? Her father is no better than an earl, though he has grand titles.
Yes, my lord, her father is a king, / The King of Naples and Jerusalem; / And of such great authority in France, / As his alliance will confirm our peace, / And keep the Frenchmen in allegiance.
Yes, my lord, her father is a king, the King of Naples and Jerusalem, and of such great power in France that an alliance with him will confirm our peace and keep the French loyal.
And so the Earl of Armagnac may do, / Because he is near kinsman unto Charles.
And so might the Earl of Armagnac, since he's a close relative of Charles.
Beside, his wealth doth warrant a liberal dower, / Where Reignier sooner will receive than give.
Besides, his wealth guarantees a generous dowry, whereas Reignier is more likely to take than give.

A dower, my lords! disgrace not so your king, / That he should be so abject, base and poor, / To choose for wealth and not for perfect love. / Henry is able to enrich his queen, / And not to seek a queen to make him rich: / So worthless peasants bargain for their wives, / As market-men for oxen, sheep, or horse. / Marriage is a matter of more worth / Than to be dealt in by attorneyship; / Not whom we will; but whom his grace affects, / Must be companion of his nuptial bed: / And therefore, lords, since he affects her most, / It most of all these reasons bindeth us, / In our opinions she should be preferr'd. / For what is wedlock forced but a hell, / An age of discord and continual strife? / Whereas the contrary bringeth bliss, / And is a pattern of celestial peace. / Whom should we match with Henry, being a king, / But Margaret, that is daughter to a king? / Her peerless feature, joined with her birth, / Approves her fit for none but for a king; / Her valiant courage and undaunted spirit, / More than in women commonly is seen, / Will answer our hope in issue of a king; / For Henry, son unto a conqueror, / Is likely to beget more conquerors, / If with a lady of so high resolve / As is fair Margaret he be link'd in love. / Then yield, my lords; and here conclude with me / That Margaret shall be queen, and none but she.

A dowry, my lords! Don't disgrace your king by making him so low, mean and poor that he chooses for money and not for true love. Henry can make his queen rich; he doesn't need to look for a queen to make him rich. That's how worthless peasants bargain for their wives, like traders for oxen, sheep or horses. Marriage is too important to be arranged by agents. Not whom we want, but whom his Grace loves, must share his marriage bed. And so, lords, since he loves her most, that reason binds us above all others to think she should be preferred. For what is forced marriage but a hell, a lifetime of quarrelling and constant strife? Whereas the opposite brings happiness and is a model of heavenly peace. Whom should we match with Henry, a king, but Margaret, the daughter of a king? Her matchless looks, together with her birth, prove her fit for no one but a king. Her brave courage and fearless spirit, greater than is commonly seen in women, will fulfil our hope for a king's heir; for Henry, son of a conqueror, is likely to father more conquerors if he is joined in love with a lady as determined as fair Margaret. So give way, my lords, and agree with me here that Margaret shall be queen, and no one but her.

Whether it be through force of your report, / My noble Lord of Suffolk, or for that / My tender youth was never yet attaint / With any passion of inflaming love, / I cannot tell; but this I am assured, / I feel such sharp dissension in my breast, / Such fierce alarums both of hope and fear, / As I am sick with working of my thoughts. / Take, therefore, shipping; post, my lord, to France; / Agree to any covenants, and procure / That Lady Margaret do vouchsafe to come / To cross the seas to England, and be crown'd / King Henry's faithful and anointed queen: / For your expenses and sufficient charge, / Among the people gather up a tenth. / Be gone, I say; for till you do return, / I rest perplexed with a thousand cares. / And you, good uncle, banish all offense: / If you do censure me by what you were, / Not what you are, I know it will excuse / This sudden execution of my will. / And so, conduct me where, from company, / I may revolve and ruminate my grief.

Whether it's the power of your report, my noble Lord of Suffolk, or because my young heart has never yet been touched by any burning love, I can't tell; but I am sure of this: I feel such sharp conflict in my heart, such fierce alarms of hope and fear, that I'm sick with the turmoil of my thoughts. So take ship; hurry to France, my lord. Agree to any terms, and make sure Lady Margaret agrees to cross the sea to England and be crowned King Henry's faithful and anointed queen. For your expenses and costs, collect a tax of a tenth from the people. Go, I say; for until you return I'll be troubled by a thousand worries. And you, good uncle, put away all offence. If you judge me by what you were when young, not by what you are now, I know it will excuse this sudden carrying out of my wishes. And so take me somewhere away from company where I can turn over and brood on my grief.
Aye, grief, I fear me, both at first and last.
Yes, grief, I'm afraid, both at the beginning and at the end.

Thus Suffolk hath prevail'd; and thus he goes, / As did the youthful Paris once to Greece, / With hope to find the like event in love, / But prosper better than the Troyan did. / Margaret shall now be queen, and rule the king; / But I will rule both her, the king and realm.

So Suffolk has won, and so he goes, as young Paris once went to Greece, hoping for a similar result in love, but to do better than the Trojan did. Margaret will now be queen and rule the King; but I will rule her, the King and the kingdom.
